# CAMPEGIUS VITRINGA
## *To the Sincere Reader*

->Greetings.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' featuring intricate floral and foliage patterns surrounding the letterform.</image-desc>

*That I, my friend the Reader, should dare to make public the thoughts of my early youth in this age of ours, and to risk my entire reputation—if indeed I have any—will, I believe, be taken poorly by many, approved of by few, and wondered at by most. For we live in an age in which very few will say what deserves praise, but almost everyone will say what deserves blame. Indeed, I have not formed such a high opinion of my own writing that I believe it could withstand the judgment of everyone. Do not think so, **Sincere Reader** <note>original: "Candide lector"; a common 17th-century greeting implying a reader who is fair-minded, honest, and well-disposed toward the author</note>, since I have observed that not even the works of the most learned of men have been able to achieve that. I am a young man, and you know how **boldness** <note>original: "audacia"</note> sometimes aids a young man, and sometimes drives him astray. I certainly would not think it has happened otherwise for me, though I have not noticed it until now. For we mortals pursue both ourselves and that which is our own with such great love that we view whatever is worthy of praise in us with sharp eyes, while that which should be blamed* <note>The sentence is interrupted here; the catchword "me-" at the bottom of the original page suggests the next word is "metuimus" (we fear) or "merito" (deservedly).</note>

<summary>In this preface, a young Campegius Vitringa introduces his work to the reader with a mixture of humility and awareness of the harsh critical environment of the late 17th century. He acknowledges that his youth and boldness may have influenced his writing and asks for a fair judgment.</summary>

PAGE 1.

## C. VITRINGA

# SACRED OBSERVATIONS.

### CHAPTER I.

->*In which the opinion concerning the confusion of languages from Genesis 11 is examined:*<-

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap letter 'V' featuring intricate floral scrollwork and a bird figure within the letter's frame.</image-desc>

Just as it is fitting that we follow with due reverence those things found to have been handed down to us by our ancestors, so also the servitude of those minds is deservedly blamed which seek arguments from those ancestors for matters in which they neither achieved, nor could have achieved, any greater certainty than our own. For although we may not possess such a great abundance or firmness of reasons that it would be necessary to withdraw from their opinion—which is venerable due to the antiquity of so many centuries—neither should their authority instill such great faith in our minds that we lose the fullest remaining freedom of thought. Indeed, if we more accurately weigh everything that various authors have written concerning the *miraculous confusion of tongues* <note>original: "confusione linguarum miraculosâ"; referring to the biblical account of the Tower of Babel in Genesis 11</note>, we do not wonder so much that they were led to this opinion by the words of Moses <note>The author of the Pentateuch, including Genesis</note>, as much as we wonder that hardly any interpreter has occurred to us so far who has dared—not indeed to remove the splendor of the miracle entirely—but to diminish it, whereas many more have dared to increase it. And certainly, we do not wish to be considered among those who would either boldly oppose the opinion believed thus far with such great consensus of minds, or the many-faceted...

## C. VITRINGA

We would be ungrateful if we disregarded the hard work and authority of learned men, or we would be stubborn <note>original: "αὐθάδεις" (Greek); meaning self-willed or arrogant</note> if we tried to force an interpretation we simply dreamed up onto others. However, we wish to bring a matter supported by the faith of so many centuries back under examination, to understand it from its very foundation and to set it forth—not so that we might tear down what was said by the Ancients on this subject, but so that we might calmly investigate those things which ought to be said. For *Isocrates* rightly says in his *Panegyric*:

*Past deeds are left to us as a common heritage, but to use them at the right time, to think properly about each, and to illustrate them with words is the specific duty of those who are wise.* <note>The author provides this quote in both the original Greek and a Latin translation to emphasize that while history belongs to everyone, interpreting it well requires skill.</note>

If we listen to Josephus, that most diligent historian of Hebrew matters <note>term: "Ebræarum Hiſtoriographum"; referring to Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish scholar whose works are a primary source for Judeo-Christian history</note>, he asserts this confusion of languages with such boldness <note>original: "παῤῥησίᾳ" (Greek); meaning frankness or total confidence</note> that the sacred text, as explained by a Jewish man drawing from the continuous tradition of the Fathers, seems to reject any opportunity for disagreement. He comments as follows in Book 1, Chapter 6 <note>In modern editions of Josephus's *Antiquities of the Jews*, this account is typically found in Book 1, Chapter 4</note>:

*Seeing them acting so insanely, God decided not to destroy them entirely—since they had not even been made wise by the first generation who perished [in the Flood]—but He threw them into discord by making them speak different languages, and by this multitude of voices caused them to be unable to understand one another. The place where they built the tower is now called Babylon; for the Hebrews call confusion "Babel."*

*Seeing this madness of theirs, God did not wish to destroy them all, since they had not even improved their character after the previous disaster: but he sent division among them by varying their languages, so that because of the diversity of speech they did not understand one another: indeed, the place in which they built the tower is now called—*

# SACRED OBSERVATIONS.

The words of Moses, which are believed to have been spoken concerning this confusion of languages, can be found in **Genesis chapter 11, verses 6 and 7**: <note>original Hebrew: ויאמר יהוה הן עם אחד ושפה אחת לכלם וזה החלם לעשות ועתה לא יבצר מהם כל אשר יזמו לעשות : הבה נרדה ונבלה שם שפתם אשר לא ישמעו איש שפת רעהו : על כן קרא שמה בבל כי שם בלל יהוה שפת כל הארץ</note> *“And the Lord said, 'Behold, the people are one and they all have one language, and this is what they begin to do; and now nothing that they propose to do will be withheld from them. Come, let us go down and there confuse their language, so that they may not understand one another’s speech.' Therefore its name was called Babel, because there the Lord confused the language of all the earth.”* These should be compared with **verse 1**: <note>original Hebrew: ויהי כל הארץ שפה אחת : ודברים אחדים</note> *“Now the whole earth was of one language and of one speech.”*

However, since it is impossible for us to approach either the interpretation or the exposition of these words before we have perceived the genuine nature of each individual term, we must first understand that nature from the very letters in which it alone exists pure and untainted. In this assessment, the word <term>Saphah <gloss>lip</gloss></term> <note>original Hebrew: שפה</note> takes the primary place. According to the constant phrasing of the Sacred Scriptures, it signifies the border or extremity of any thing, and from this, the *lip*. Examples are found everywhere. The <term>Seventy <gloss>The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Old Testament</gloss></term> translate this as <term>cheilos <gloss>lip</gloss></term> <note>original Greek: χεῖλος</note> and <term>glossa <gloss>tongue</gloss></term> <note>original Greek: γλῶσσα</note>.

But because the *lip*, as the extremity of the mouth, is a significant instrument of human speech, the sacred writers—who held the authority over how things were expressed—sometimes (indeed, many times) used this word <term>Saphah <gloss>lip</gloss></term> for *speech*, *discourse*, or not just a dialect of speaking, but the very *sentiment* or *meaning* of the thing said. Because we are laying this very point down as the foundation for our interpretation, it must be demonstrated at somewhat greater length. 

An excellent passage exists in **Zephaniah, chapter 3, verse 9**: <note>original Hebrew: כי אז אהפך אל עמים שפה ברורה</note> *“For then I will return to the peoples a pure language”* <note>The author translates the Hebrew phrase 'Saphah Berurah' as 'select lip' or 'chosen speech.'</note>. It should be noted in passing <note>original Greek phrase: ἐν παρόδῳ (en parodō)</note> that the <term>Seventy <gloss>The Septuagint translators</gloss></term> clearly went astray here, as they translated it: *“For then I will change the tongue for the people to its generation.”* <note>original Greek: ὅτι τότε μεταστρέψω ἐπὶ λαοὺς γλῶσσαν εἰς γενεὰν αὐτῆς</note> *Then*...

# C. VITRINGA

“...for I will turn to the peoples a language in that age,” <note>This refers to a translation of Zephaniah 3:9. The standard reading is “a pure language/lip,” but some versions rendered it as “in that age.”</note> as the version has it: this error certainly arose from no other source than that they read <term>bedor <gloss>in a generation/age</gloss></term> <note>Hebrew: בְּדוֹר</note> instead of what we have, <term>berurah <gloss>pure</gloss></term>, <note>Hebrew: בְּרוּרָה</note> due to a very easy swapping of the letters **D** (ד) and **R** (ר), which frequently occurs in other places as well. <note>In the Hebrew alphabet, Dalet (ד) and Resh (ר) are nearly identical, differing only by a slight corner, making them the most common source of scribal copying errors.</note> But just as the Greek version shows that the Hebrew context had been corrupted, so the Latin translation corrupted the Greek. For the phrase “into a generation” <note>Greek: εις γενεὰν</note> should not have been transposed here as *into an age*, but as *in an age*, according to the frequent use of that particle when the letter **B** (ב) corresponds to it among the Hebrews.

Furthermore, although the <term>paraphrase <gloss>interpretive summary</gloss></term> of these words is quite varied, no interpreters have yet emerged who explained the word <term>Saphah <gloss>lip/language</gloss></term> in this passage as a "dialect," if you except only **Aben Ezra**, <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a major Spanish Jewish scholar and biblical exegete.</note> who indulges in the fictions of his ancestors: <note>original Hebrew: יתהפכו לעבוד השם לבדו : בשפה ברורה היא לשון הקדש שבה לבדה נקרא השם הנכבד:</note> *“They shall be converted,”* he says, *“to serving God alone with a pure lip; this is the holy language, in which alone the honored God is named.”* Truly, the Hebrew progeny is so in love with its own rituals and its own *fabrications* that they wish to see them established everywhere, even when the sacred prophecies cry out that all those things were to be abolished with the coming of the Messiah—a truth to which the most blessed outcome has responded. 

Therefore, **David Kimchi** <note>Also known as Radak (1160–1235), a prominent rabbi and grammarian whose commentaries are central to Jewish tradition.</note> is more correct, as he occasionally allows his mind to yield to the truth rather than to pleasant-sounding words: <note>original Hebrew: פי׳ העמים שישארו אחר מלחמת גוג שפתם : הראשונה אהפך אותה לשפה ברורה שלא יוציאו בשפתם אלהים אחרים אלא כולם יקראו בשם ה׳ והו׳ שפה ברורה כמו שאמר בנבואת זכריה ביום ההוא יהיה ה׳ אחד ושמו אחד :</note> *“The explanation is: That the speech of the peoples who will remain after the war of Gog, which was their first speech, I will change into a pure speech, so that they do not utter other gods with their lips, but they shall all call upon the name of the Lord; and this 'pure speech' is as he said in the prophecy of Zechariah: 'In that day the Lord shall be one, and His name one.'”*

### C. VITRINGA

...to the reason of the Hebrews, and the vowel points of the holy language also correspond to the matters being discussed, so that no difficulty remains:

But perhaps we have wandered too far from our intended purpose. Another passage falters:
<margin>lip <note>original: labium</note></margin> **Proverbs 12:19**: *The lip of truth shall be established forever.* <note>Hebrew: שְׂפַת־אֱמֶת תִּכּוֹן לָעַד (Saphath-emeth tikhon la'ad).</note> If you should wish to explain this in terms of a **dialect** <note>original Latin: "dialecto," referring to a specific language like Hebrew or Greek.</note> of speech, you would rightly show yourself to be someone who should not be refuted, but laughed at. Therefore, **Aben-Ezra** <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a distinguished Spanish Jewish scholar and biblical commentator.</note> rightly interprets:
<margin>speech <note>original: loquela</note></margin> *The lip of truth* in this place as *a testimony of truth* <note>original Hebrew: עֵדוּת אֱמֶת (edut emeth).</note>. Similarly, **Rabbi Levi ben Gerson** <note>Also known as Gersonides (1288–1344), a French Jewish philosopher and commentator.</note> interprets it as *a word, speech, or oration of truth* <note>original Hebrew: דְּבַר אֱמֶת (devar emeth).</note>, which is the simplest interpretation and most consistent with the tenor of Holy Scripture. You find a similar construction in:
<margin>lip <note>original: labium</note></margin> *The lip of iniquity* <note>Hebrew: שְׂפַת אָוֶן (Saphath aven).</note> in **Proverbs 17:4**, and *The lip of flatteries* <note>Hebrew: שְׂפַת חֲלָקוֹת (Saphath chalakot).</note> in **Psalm 12:3**. We could add more arguments for this meaning, were it not that we believe a few examples are plainly sufficient to demonstrate this truth.

Indeed, it would not be difficult for us to prove that no testimonies occur in the sacred writings from which this meaning—so commonly attributed to this word by everyone—could be forced, if the context is examined with reason. But because perhaps no greater strength would be added to our exposition from this, it will suffice to add one thing: the sacred writers are accustomed to express the **dialect of speech and language** through the word *Lashon* <note>Hebrew: לָשׁוֹן (tongue).</note> in those places where it is clear to all that they are dealing with dialects, and not with the meanings of orations or speeches. Because the word *Lashon* is not found in this entire chapter, where many nevertheless judge that "languages" and the idioms of speech are being discussed, I am rightly suspicious whether the word *Saphah* [lip] should be [translated] as *idiom* or *dialect*...

<page-num>11</page-num>

# HOLY OBSERVATIONS.

It should be explained on this occasion, since it truly seems most likely that the Holy Spirit used such a word here which expresses <term>dialect</term> <note>original Latin: dialectum</note> most precisely, and wished us to understand that a *confusion of dialects* <note>original Latin: confusionem dialectorum</note> occurred here. We say and understand this with reverence, for we are not the ones to prescribe limits to the all-wise Spirit. Thus, we find *The tongue of the Chaldeans* <note>Hebrew: לשון כשדים (Lashon Kasdim)</note> in **Daniel 1:4**; and *to every people according to their own dialect* <note>Hebrew: ואל עם ועם בלשונו (ve-el am va-am bi-lshono); Latin: secundum dialectum suam</note>; and *speaking according to the dialect of his own people* <note>Hebrew: ומדבר כלשון עמו (u-medabber ki-lshon ammo); Latin: secundum dialectum populi sui</note>.

The Greeks also constantly used the terms <term>tongue</term> <note>Greek: γλῶσσα (glossa)</note> or <term>dialect</term> <note>Greek: διάλεκτος (dialektos)</note>, but never, as far as I am aware, did they use the word <term>lip</term> <note>Greek: χεῖλος (cheilos)</note> in this context. The Apostle also follows this way of speaking in **1 Corinthians 14:11**, where he treats a related argument concerning the use of variety in languages within the early <term>Christian Church</term>. Thus, he speaks of *one who speaks in a tongue* <note>Greek: ὁ λαλῶν γλώσσῃ (ho lalon glosse)</note>, *to speak in tongues* <note>Greek: λαλεῖν γλώσσαις (lalein glossais); Hebrew equivalent: דבר בלשונות (dabber bi-lshonot)</note>, *I may pray with a tongue* <note>Greek: προσεύχωμαι γλώσσῃ (proseuchomai glosse)</note>, *with other tongues* <note>Greek: ἑτερογλώσσοις (heteroglossais)</note>, and many more examples that exist.

Nor should we wonder that the Apostle does not use the word *dialect* <note>Greek: διάλεκτος (dialektos)</note> in this entire passage, since the purer Greek writers observed a certain distinction between *tongue* <note>Greek: γλῶσσα (glossa)</note> and *dialect* <note>Greek: διάλεκτος (dialektos)</note>. Let <term>Clement of Alexandria</term> <note>Titus Flavius Clemens (c. 150–215 AD), an early Christian theologian who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with Scripture.</note> instruct us on this matter, whose opinion is worthy of being recorded; thus he writes in his *Stromata* <note>A work titled "Miscellanies," which functions as a tapestry of various philosophical and theological ideas.</note>, Book 1:

> It appears that according to the true account, the general **Dialects** are seventy-two in number <note>The number seventy-two refers to the traditional number of nations and languages stemming from the descendants of Noah after the Tower of Babel.</note>, as our scriptures hand down; the many others arise from the meeting of two or three or even more **Dialects**. A **Dialect** is a form of speech expressing the specific character of a place, or a form of speech showing the specific or common character of a nation. The Greeks say that however many the voices of the barbarians are, they are not to be called **Dialects**, but **Tongues**.

<header>C. VITRINGA</header>

*It seems, however, from the true reasoning of dialects, that there are seventy-two general languages and speeches, as our scriptures hand down: Others, moreover, are formed through the mixing of two or three, or even more dialects: A dialect, however, is a way of speaking that shows the character specific to a place: or a way of speaking that shows the specific or common character of a nation: The Greeks say, moreover, that the voices of barbarians, which cannot be understood, are not called dialects, but languages:* <note>original Latin: "Videntur autem ex verà ratione dialecti..." This italicized section appears to be a citation from an ancient authority, possibly Clement of Alexandria, defining the traditional number of 72 nations and their tongues.</note>

With these things established in this way, I think I may safely conclude—unless some specific reason in the Mosaic context (which we previously proved must be uniquely trusted in explaining these words) suggests the contrary, and if the nature of the matter itself and the <term>analogy</term> <note>Greek: ἀναλογία (analogia); the theological principle that one part of Scripture should be interpreted in harmony with the rest</note> of the other scriptures do not require something else—that the meaning of the word <term>lip</term> <note>Hebrew: שפה (Saphah)</note> can be maintained here, which is not only its common but also its familiar use: which has been demonstrated thus far.

It is indeed true that the universal opinion of the commentators of the Hebrew nation by no means fits this explanation of the word in this place, nor do the foundations of our interpretation require it; nevertheless, we do not hesitate to say that things are found in their ancient monuments which teach that the word <term>lip</term> <note>Hebrew: שפה (Saphah)</note> in this passage was explained by them as *speech*, *oration*, or *opinion*: We have that ancient commentary on the five books of Moses called *Tanchuma*, or *Yelammedenu* <note>A famous collection of Jewish homilies or "Midrash" dating back to the early medieval period</note>, where in the <term>Parashah</term> <note>The weekly portion of the Torah read in the synagogue</note> which is inscribed <term>The Generations of Noah</term> <note>Hebrew: תולדות נח (Toledot Noach); refers to Genesis 6:9–11:32</note>, in the explanation of the words <term>one lip</term> <note>Hebrew: שפה אחת (Saphah achat); Genesis 11:1</note>, this discourse is established:

> They said: "It is not within His power <note>referring to God</note> to choose for Himself the upper realms and give us the lower realms. Let us go up to the firmament and strike it with axes"; they were divided into three <insert>groups</insert> <note>original Hebrew: כתות (kittot)</note>.

<meta>This page continues Vitringa’s philological investigation into the Hebrew root DBR (דבר). On the previous page, he began exploring whether this term, often translated as "words" in Genesis 11:1, might have a deeper, primary meaning related to guidance or direction rather than just vocalized speech.</meta>

<page-num>14</page-num>

<header>C. VITRINGA</header>

[This] suggests that it is distinct [from the previous point], although our <margin>hypothesis <note>original Greek: ὑπόθεσις</note></margin> would otherwise not be opposed to it. It is necessary, therefore, that we understand this point from another source. We shall understand it easily if we carefully weigh those themes which everyone admits descend from the radical root <term>דבר <note>DBR</note></term>, but which nevertheless can in no way be reduced to the meaning of "speaking" or "saying."

For example:
* <term>מדבר <note>midbar</note></term> means a *wilderness* or *desert*.
* <term>דבר <note>dever</note></term> means a *sheepfold*.
* <term>דבורה <note>deborah</note></term> means an *intention* or *aim*.
* <term>דבורה <note>deborah</note></term> also means a *bee*.
* <term>דברות <note>dovrot</note></term> means *rafts*.

What do these have in common with *discourse* or *speech*? If, therefore, we find a meaning for the root <term>דבר <note>DBR</note></term> in which all these other examples we have just reviewed agree most precisely, then we must say we have finally discovered its true and genuine sense.

We believe, therefore, that in <margin>Verse 1</margin> the root <term>דבר <note>DBR</note></term> primarily signifies not *discourse* or speech, but a *leading* or *guidance* <note>Latin: ductum</note>. Because there is a certain *leading* or *flow* involved in the arrangement of various thoughts, as well as in the speech of the throat, mouth, and tongue—indeed, in the very passage of speech through the <margin>throat</margin>, mouth, and tongue—the word corresponds to the <term>Greek word "lego" <note>τῷ λέγω; usually meaning "to say," but originally "to gather or arrange"</note></term>, and indicates both *reason* and *speech*. 

From this same root, we get <term>מדבר <note>midbar</note></term> for *wilderness* and <term>דבר <note>dever</note></term> for *sheepfold*, because into both of these there is a *leading* of cattle. This applies to the other themes we reviewed as well, in which we observe a *leading* of either art or nature <note>e.g., bees following a leader, or rafts being guided through water</note>. Thus, regarding <margin>Verse 1</margin>, *Moses of Gerona* <note>also known as Nachmanides, a major medieval Jewish scholar</note> translates the word <term>דברות <note>dovrot</note></term> as <term>הנהגת <note>hanhagat</note></term>, meaning *guidance* or *intention*. 

To the Chaldeans <note>speakers of Aramaic</note>, this meaning is so familiar that they have almost no other for this word. The same must be said of the Syrians and Arabs. Thus, in *Numbers 23:14*: <term>וידבריה <note>va-yedabberehu</note></term> is rendered in Aramaic as <term>לחקל סכותא <note>le-hakal sakhuta</note></term>, meaning: *And he led him into the field of the watchmen*. In *Exodus 13:21*: <term>לדברותהון באורחא <note>le-davrotehon be-orkha</note></term> means: *To lead them in the way*. We see the same in the Greek of Saint Matthew, chapter 4:1: <term>Then Jesus was led up into the wilderness by the Spirit <note>original Greek: Τότε ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἀνήχθη εἰς τὴν ἔρημον ὑπὸ τοῦ πνεύματος</note></term>.

<page-num>15</page-num>
<header>SACRED OBSERVATIONS.</header>

The *Syriac* <note>The Syriac Peshitta, an ancient translation of the Bible</note> has rendered this most excellently: <note>original Aramaic: הֵידֵין יֵשׁוּע אִתְדְבַר מִן רוּחָא דְקוּדְשָא לְמַדְבּרָא</note> *Then Jesus was led by the Holy Spirit into the desert*. Given these suppositions, we say that the term <term>debarim <note>Hebrew: דְּבָרִים, usually translated as "words"</note></term> does not simply signify *discourses*, in such a way that it would be indistinguishable from <term>sephah <note>Hebrew: שְׂפָה, literally "lip," meaning language</note></term>. Rather, it denotes those types of *discourses* and *words* in which there is a certain <term>kavanah <note>Hebrew: כַּוָּנָה</note></term> or *intention*, a certain *direction*, and a specific goal. It also refers to that very *direction* and intention which is expressed through the words and discourses.

Indeed, the word <term>dibrati <note>Hebrew: דְּבָרַי, a form of the root DBR</note></term> carries this same meaning in *Job 5:8*: <note>original Hebrew: אוּלָם אֲנִי אֶדְרֹשׁ אֶל אֵל וְאֶל אֱלֹהִים אָשִׂים דִּבְרָתִי</note> *Truly, I would seek after the mighty God, and to God I would set my intention*. The *Chaldean* <note>The Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> translator here rendered <term>dibrati</term> as <term>millati <note>Aramaic: מִלְּתִי</note></term> or *my word*. However, we may safely say that in many places, he either did not understand the genius of the Hebrew dialect itself, or he preferred the <term>tradition <note>original Greek: παράδοσιν</note></term> of his ancestors. This very verse could demonstrate that: for the first part of this phrase, "Truly I would seek after the mighty God," he translated as: <note>original Aramaic: בְּרַם אֲנָא אֶתְבְּעֵי אוּלְפָן מִן תַּקִּיפָא</note> *But I would seek doctrine from the Mighty One*. This arose from nothing other than that meaning of the word <term>darash <note>Hebrew: דָּרַשׁ, to seek or inquire</note></term> which is most familiar to the teachers <note>The Rabbinic sages</note>.

And truly, we seem to find traces of this observation in the ancient commentaries of the Hebrews, who explained <term>debarim</term> as *counsel* or *plan*. *Solomon Jarchi* <note>Better known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French rabbi and commentator</note> records almost the same words that we previously cited from the *Tanchuma* <note>A collection of ancient Jewish homilies</note> regarding the word *sephah*; regarding the interpretation of *debarim* from *Bereshit Rabba* <note>An ancient midrashic commentary on Genesis</note>, he himself yields to this same opinion. For he notes regarding the phrase *after these things* <note>Hebrew: אַחֲרֵי דְּבָרֵי, Genesis 15:1 or 22:1</note>: *They came to the same [conclusion]...*

<header>C. VITRINGA</header>

[The previous context] commands that this word be distinct [from the other], although it would not otherwise be opposed to our **conception** <gloss>original Greek: ἐννοίᾳ (ennoia)</gloss>. It is necessary, therefore, that we understand this from elsewhere. We shall easily understand it if we weigh those themes which everyone admits descend from the radical root <term>Davar</term> <note>Hebrew: דבר; the root D-B-R typically associated with "speaking," but Vitringa is searching for a more primary meaning</note>, and which nevertheless can in no way be reduced to the meaning of *speaking* or *saying*.

For example:
*   <term>Midbar</term> <note>Hebrew: מדבר</note> meaning *desert*
*   <term>Dover</term> <note>Hebrew: דבר</note> meaning *fold* or *pasture*
*   <term>Devorah</term> <note>Hebrew: דבורה</note> meaning *intention* or *purpose*
*   <term>Devorah</term> <note>Hebrew: דבורה</note> meaning *bee*
*   <term>Dovrot</term> <note>Hebrew: דברות</note> meaning *rafts*

What do these have in common with *speech* or *discourse*? If, therefore, we find such a meaning for <term>Davar</term> in which all the others just listed most carefully agree, then we must say we have finally found the true and genuine one.

We believe, therefore, that the word <term>Davar</term> <note>Hebrew: τὸ דבר</note> primarily signifies not *discourse* or *speech*, but **guidance** or **leading** <note>Latin: ductum; a "leading along" or "direction"</note>. Because there is a certain *guidance* in the **logic** of various thoughts, and in the speech of the throat, mouth, and tongue—indeed, even in the "leading" of the speech itself through the throat, mouth, and tongue—it corresponds for this reason to the word <term>Logos</term> <note>Greek: λόγῳ; meaning both "word" and "reason/logic"</note> and indicates both *reason* and *speech*.

From this comes <term>Midbar</term> (*desert*) and <term>Dover</term> (*fold*), because there is a *leading* of cattle into both; and it applies to the other themes we have reviewed and which exist, in which we contemplate a "leading" either by art or by nature. Thus, **Moses Gerundensis** <note>Also known as Nachmanides or Ramban, a leading medieval Jewish scholar (1194–1270)</note> translates the word <term>Devorah</term> <note>Hebrew: דבורה</note> as **guidance** or **intention** <note>Hebrew: הנהגת (hanhagah)</note>.

Certainly, this meaning is so familiar to the Chaldeans <note>Aramaic speakers/translators</note> that they have almost no other for this word. The same must be said of the Syrians and Arabs. Thus, in **Numbers 23:14**: *And he led him* <note>Chaldaic/Aramaic: ודבריה (u-davrei); standard Hebrew would use a different root for "led"</note> *to the field of observation*. And **Exodus 13:21**: *To lead them* <note>Chaldaic/Aramaic: לדברוחהון (le-davruhon)</note> *on the way*. In the same way, the Greek of Saint Matthew says in chapter 4:1:

->*Then Jesus was led up into the desert by the Spirit,*<-

The *Syriac* <note>The Peshitta, an ancient Syriac translation of the Bible</note> translated this excellently: **Then Jesus was led by the Holy Spirit into the desert.** <note>original Syriac: הידין ישוע אתדבר מן רוחא דקודשא למדברא</note> Given these points, we say that <term>דברים <note>debarim - usually "words"</note></term> does not simply signify *speeches*, such that it would be in no way distinguished from <term>שפה <note>shapah - "lip" or "language"</note></term>; but rather, it denotes speeches of such a kind—words of such a kind—in which there is a certain <term>כונה <note>kavanah</note> intention</term>, a certain *direction*, and a particular *aim*. It even refers to that very direction and intention which is expressed through the words and speeches. Indeed, the word <term>דברתי <note>dibrati</note></term> has this same meaning in *Job 5:8*: **But as for me, I would seek (I would pray, I would direct myself) to the strong God, and to God I would set my intention.** <note>original Hebrew: אולם אני אדרש אל אל ואל אלהים אשים דברתי</note> 

The *Chaldean* <note>The Aramaic Targum, an ancient Jewish translation and paraphrase</note> translated <term>דברתי <note>dibrati</note></term> here as <term>מלתי <note>milti</note> my word</term>; but we may say without penalty that in many places the translator either did not understand the character of the Hebrew dialect itself, or he preferred the <term>traditions <note>original Greek: παραδόσεις</note></term> of his ancestors. This very verse could teach us this: for he translated the first part of this phrase, **But as for me, I would seek the strong God**, as **But I will seek instruction from the Strong One.** <note>original Aramaic: ברם אנא אתבעי אולפן מן תקיפא</note> This arose from no other source than that meaning of the word <term>דרש <note>darash</note> to seek or inquire</term> which is most familiar to the Masters <note>the Rabbinic sages</note>.

And indeed, we seem to find traces of this observation in the ancient commentaries of the Hebrews, who explained <term>דברים <note>debarim</note></term> as *counsel* or *purpose*. *Solomon Iarchi* <note>The famous medieval commentator Rashi</note> relates almost the same words that we previously cited from the *Tanchuma* <note>A collection of homiletic teachings</note> regarding the word <term>שפה <note>shapah</note></term> for the interpretation of <term>דברים <note>debarim</note></term> from *Bereshit Rabba* <note>An ancient commentary on Genesis</note>, and he himself adopts this same opinion. Thus he notes regarding the phrase "The words after" <note>likely referring to the "one language and few words" of the Tower of Babel in Genesis 11:1</note>: *They came into the same coun-* <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "confi-", likely leading into "consilium" (counsel)</note>

Similar accounts are found in the *Rabboth* <note>The *Midrash Rabbah*, a collection of ancient Jewish commentaries on the Hebrew Bible</note>, on folio 31. I have little doubt that this tasteless <term>translation</term> <note>original Greek: μετάφρασις (metaphrasis)</note> took its origin from a faulty interpretation of the small word *Shem* <note>original Hebrew: שם (Shem), meaning "Name," often interpreted as "reputation" or "monument" in the context of the Tower of Babel</note>; but I also believe that no small occasion was given for this fabrication by everything that various authors have left us regarding the *Temple of Bel* <note>Bel, or Marduk, was the patron deity of Babylon</note>. <header>C. VITRINGA</header>

For that reason, having explained the emphasis <term>ἐμφάσει</term> <note>original Greek: emphasis; referring to the specific nuance or force of a word</note> of the word *lip* <note>original Hebrew: שפה (shaphah)</note>, it remains for us to explain *confound* and *Babel* <note>original Hebrew: בלל (balal) and בבל (Babel)</note>, so that we may finally bring forth their genuine meaning. There is no doubt that *Babel* ought to be referred to *balal* [to confound]; for the conjecture of *Aben-Ezra* <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a celebrated Spanish Jewish scholar and biblical commentator</note>—that *Babel* was as if it were *Ba Bel*, meaning "confusion comes"—was long ago exploded [rejected] by learned men. Indeed, there exists an excellent dissertation on this matter by *Johannes Drusius* <note>Jan van den Driesche (1550–1616), a Flemish Protestant scholar renowned for his expertise in Hebrew and Aramaic</note>, a man most skilled in sacred lexicography <term>λεξικῇ</term> <note>original Greek: lexike; the study of word meanings and dictionaries</note>. "The Chaldeans," he says, "say *balbel* <note>original Aramaic: בלבל</note> for what in Hebrew is *balal* <note>original Hebrew: בלל</note>, 'he confounded,' from which comes *balbul* <note>original Aramaic: בלבול</note>, 'confusion.' Therefore, *Babel* seems to be said as if it were *Balbel*, with one letter removed, just as in *Golgotha*, which they pronounced in the time of Christ instead of *Golgoltha*, that is, 'the skull' or 'cranium.' The Syrian translator has *gagultha*; in both cases, the second letter is dropped, just as when they say *Kaceltha* <note>original Aramaic: קקלתא</note> or *Kikheltha* <note>original Aramaic: קיקלתא</note>, meaning dung or a dunghill. You will find this in the *Talmud*, in the treatise *On Foreign Worship* <note>The tractate Avodah Zarah, which deals with laws regarding interactions with pagans</note>, folio 28, page 1. Moreover, in the *Targum* <note>Ancient Aramaic translations or paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible</note>, *ashpatha* <note>original Aramaic: אשפתא; meaning ash-heap or dunghill</note> stands for this in the Hebrew text. However, it is read in full as *kakeltha* in 1 Samuel 2. Similarly, for the sake of brevity, *darah* <note>original Hebrew/Aramaic: דרה</note> is written for *dibrah* <note>original Hebrew/Aramaic: דברה</note>, 'he magnified,' from which comes *itdarah*, 'he was magnified.' And thus far speaks the most learned Drusius."

Therefore, *balal* carries the meaning of confusion <term>συγχύσεως</term> <note>original Greek: synchyseos</note>, that is, of 'confusion and mixing,' from which *Babel* was called "Confusion" <term>σύγχυσις</term> <note>original Greek: synchysis</note> by *Josephus* <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</note> and the *Seventy* <note>The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Old Testament</note. And although everyone acknowledges this meaning, no one seems to me to have correctly applied it to this matter of *speech*. For they have supposed that *languages* were confounded here, even though they themselves admit there were no languages at that time except Hebrew, and although the sacred text asserts that it was the *lip* or *speech* that was confounded. In this passage, they constantly seek the origin of multiple languages, of which there is not even a single word in the entire Mosaic narrative. Therefore, the matter must be dug up from its foundations, so that we may finally understand what *balal* [to confound] signifies.

<summary>Campegius Vitringa discusses the etymological origins of the name "Babel," citing Johannes Drusius to explain how linguistic contraction turned "Balbel" into "Babel." He argues that traditional interpretations mistakenly focus on the creation of multiple languages rather than the confusion of "speech" or "lips" mentioned in the biblical text.</summary>

...if it has its own relation to the *lip* <note>original Hebrew: שפה (shaphah)</note>, or *speech*: But, since the sacred scriptures suggest almost nothing to me from which I could explain the *force* <term>ἐνέργειαν</term> <note>original Greek: energeian; referring to the active power or literal effect of the word</note> of that phrasing, I must primarily attend to what it is that finally unfolds clearly and distinctly in my mind and is approved by my *internal perception* <term>συνειδήσει</term> <note>original Greek: syneidesei; here meaning one's consciousness or intuitive understanding</note> when I hear that *the lip or speech of man is confounded*: I certainly cannot bring myself to believe that either the *lip* or the *speech* or the *tongue* (if you prefer to interpret the little word *shaphah* that way) is then confounded when it is divided into many. Nor do I believe that the Hebrew dialect—which some argue is the one mentioned in this passage—was confounded at that time simply because many others arose besides it; for the Hebrew language remained even then, and is still to this day the most perfect of all.

Rather, the first thing that enters my thoughts when I perceive that *a lip or speech has been confounded* is either that *the lip of the speaker was moved in a disorderly fashion* or that *the speech itself was confusedly pronounced*. And what if other dialects were to come to our aid here? We have indeed, among the Latins, the words *Balbus* <note>meaning a stammerer or stutterer</note> and *Balbutio* <note>meaning to stutter or speak unclearly</note>. How weak is the suggestion of *Numesius* <note>A reference to a grammarian; likely an error for a classical author or a specific contemporary philologist</note> in his grammar that the word *balbus* is derived from the Greek *psellos* <note>original Greek: ψελλὸς; meaning one who stammers or speaks indistinctly</note>, which carries the same meaning for the Greeks? How much better it is to derive it from the Hebrew/Aramaic *balbel* or *balbul* <note>original Hebrew/Aramaic: בבל / בלבל / בלביל</note>, meaning *stammerer*; and to suggest that the Latin *balbutire* [to stutter] was used instead of *balbulire* by a very easy *transposition of letters* <term>μεταθέσει</term> <note>original Greek: metathesi; a linguistic process where sounds or letters are swapped within a word</note>?

Nay more, from this very word *Babel* <note>original Hebrew: בבל</note> comes the Dutch word *babbelen* <note>meaning to babble or chatter</note>. Whence you would say in Hebrew "he babbles" as *he makes his tongue vile* <note>original Hebrew: נבל לשונו (nabal leshono)</note> or *our lip* <note>original Hebrew: שפתנו (shaphathenu)</note>. This is also the Greek *baubazein* <note>original Greek: βαυβάζειν; to speak inarticulately</note>, meaning *I speak inarticulately, I babble, I babble* <note>original Dutch/German: ich babbele</note>; and *bambalizo* <note>original Greek: βαμβαλίζω; to stammer</note>, used instead of *barbarizo* <note>original Greek: βαρβαρίζω; to speak like a foreigner or "barbarian"</note>.

<meta>This page continues the philological investigation into the name "Babel" and the linguistic "confusion" described in Genesis. Having previously discussed the physiological aspect of the "lip," the author now explores the etymological roots of the word Babel itself, comparing it to other phonetic contractions in ancient languages.</meta>

<page-num>20</page-num>
<header>C. VITRINGA</header>

For the reason explained by the emphasis <note>original Greek: ἐμφάσει (emphasei)</note> of the word Babel [בבל], there remains to be explained the roots *balal* and *balbel* [בלל & בלבל] through which we may finally bring forth their genuine meaning. There is no doubt that *Babel* is referred back to the root *balal*; for the conjecture of *Aben-Ezra* <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a renowned 12th-century Jewish scholar and grammarian</note>—that *Babel* was actually *ba bel*, meaning "confusion comes"—has long since been rejected by learned men. There exists, in fact, an excellent dissertation on this matter by *Johannes Drusius* <note>Jan Drusius (1550–1616), a Flemish Protestant scholar and expert in Semitic languages</note>, a man most practiced in sacred matters. 

The Chaldeans <note>referring here to speakers of Aramaic</note>, he says, use the word *balbel*, which in Hebrew is *balal*, meaning "he confounded" or "he mixed," and *balbul*, meaning "confusion." It seems, therefore, that *Babel* was named as if it were *Balbal*, with one letter worn away <note>a linguistic process called elision or haplography, where similar sounds are dropped for ease of speech</note>, just as in the word *Golgotha*, which was pronounced that way in the time of Christ instead of *Golgoltha*—meaning: 1. a cranium or skull. The Syriac interpreter <note>The Peshitta, an ancient Syriac translation of the Bible</note> has it as *gagultha*. In both cases, a letter is missing, just as when they say *Kaceltha* [קקלתא] or *Kilhetha* [קילקתא] for a dunghill or refuse heap. You will find this in the Talmud, in the treatise *Concerning a Strange Debt*, folio 28, page 1. But it is also found in the Targum <note>ancient Aramaic paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible</note> in place of what is in the Hebrew text; it is read in its full form, however, as *qalqaltha* [קלקלתא] in 1 Samuel 28 <note>Likely referring to 1 Samuel 2:8, where the "dunghill" is mentioned</note>. Similarly, for the sake of brevity, *rab* [רב] is written for *rarab* [ררב], meaning "he made great," from which comes *athrab* [אתרב], "he was magnified." 

Thus far speaks the most learned *Drusius*. The word *Babel*, therefore, holds the significance of "confusion" or "mixture" <note>original Greek: συγχύσεως (synchyseōs)</note>, which is why *Babel* was called *synchysis* <note>original Greek: σύγχυσις; a blending or pouring together</note> by Josephus <note>Titus Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian</note> and the Septuagint <note>the "Seventy" (ἑβδομήκοντα), referring to the earliest Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>. 

And although everyone acknowledges this meaning, no one, it seems to me, has correctly applied it to this specific subject of *speech*. For many have estimated that *languages* were confounded here, even though they themselves admit that no languages existed at that time except for Hebrew. Furthermore, the sacred text itself asserts that it was the *lip* or the *speech* that was confounded. Scholars constantly seek the origin of multiple languages in this passage, yet not a single word regarding that is contained in the entire Mosaic narrative. From this, it appears the matter must be dug up from its foundations, so that we may finally understand what *Babel* truly signifies.

<page-num>22</page-num>
<header>C. VITRINGA</header>

which is so directly referred to *Balbal* <note>original Hebrew: בלבל, meaning to mix, mingle, or confuse</note>: *Hesychius* <note>An influential 5th-century Greek lexicographer</note> defines *bambalei* <note>original Greek: βαμβάλει</note> as: *to tremble, or to make a clattering sound with the lips*; and *bambainon* <note>original Greek: βαμβαίνων</note> as: *trembling in the feet, or chattering the teeth*. In Dutch: **bibbert** is used instead of **bibbelt** <note>Vitringa is noting a dialectical or phonetic shift in the Dutch words for shivering or trembling</note>. To this same origin, it seems to me, we should trace the word *babazo* <note>original Greek: βαβάζω</note>, which the same *Hesychius* explains as *to speak inarticulately* <note>original Greek: τὸ μὴ διηρθρωμένα λέγω</note>, unless we establish the primary theme to be *bazo* <note>original Greek: βάζω, meaning to speak or say</note>, as lexicographers commonly do. But what if we were to proceed with such boldness as to say that the word *babazo* is derived from this very same word בלבל (*Balbal*)? And that **barbaros** <note>original Greek: βάρβαρος; the root of the English word "barbarian"</note> was said instead of **balbalos**? This is even more likely if we consider how much those who have—not unsuccessfully—uncovered the origins of words have struggled with this theme. One can see this in the works of the most learned *Vossius* <note>Gerardus Johannes Vossius (1577–1649), a titan of classical scholarship</note> in his commentaries on this word, though perhaps even he did not use his full <term>precision of judgment</term> <note>original Greek: ἀκριβείᾳ (akribeia)</note> here. 

Indeed, no one can doubt that the letters **L** <note>Hebrew: ל</note> and **R** <note>Hebrew: ר</note> are very frequently swapped for one another. Thus, *kephalargia* <note>original Greek: κεφαλαργία</note> was said by the Attics <note>the people of ancient Athens</note> instead of *kephalalgia* <note>original Greek: κεφαλαλγία, meaning headache</note>; *kribanos* <note>original Greek: κρίβανο</note> for *klibanos* <note>original Greek: κλίβανο, an earthenware oven</note>. Among the Latins, *Ceruleus* <note>sky blue</note> was used for what the ancients called *calulius*. Similarly, *Samuel Bochart* <note>A 17th-century scholar of biblical geography and animals</note> demonstrates in his work *On the Phoenician Colonies* (Book 1, Chapter 33) that *Italia* <note>Italy</note> was said for *Itaria*, or וטריא. Thus (he says), in *Spain*, *Tavila* is *Tavira* <note>original Arabic: טבירה</note> in Arabic. In *Corsica*, *Alalia* and *Aleria* are the same place. In *Sardinia*, *Caralis* and *Canalis*. In *Boeotia*, *Aliarthus* and *Ariarthus*. Many more examples of this <term>permutation</term> <note>the systematic swapping of sounds in different dialects</note> exist in that same work. 

To these we add that it is especially noteworthy that this exchange of letters sometimes occurred in this very word בלבל (*Balbal*) itself. Thus, *Balbalutha* <note>original Hebrew: בלבלותא</note> in the tractate *Bechoroth* <note>a section of the Talmud dealing with firstborn animals</note> is written in the *Aruch* <note>a famous 11th-century dictionary of the Talmud and Midrash</note> as *Barbarutha* <note>original Hebrew: ברבלותא</note>; from which...

we conclude that we say nothing alien to sound reason when we demonstrate that *bambalo* <note>original Greek: βάμβαλο; a word mimicking the sound of shivering or stuttering</note> was changed into *barbaro*: a **barbarian**, moreover, is one whom I do not understand when they speak, and who seems to me to stutter, or to produce an inarticulate sound. *Hesychius* <note>The 5th-century lexicographer mentioned on the previous page</note> interprets "barbarian" less correctly as "uneducated" <note>original Greek: ἀπαίδευτον (*apaideuton*)</note>, since it is certain that the Barbarians also flourished greatly in the glory of wisdom. "Philosophy, therefore, a most useful thing, flourished long ago among the **BARBARIANS**, shining throughout the nations. Later, it also came down to the Greeks. Those who presided over it were the Prophets of the Egyptians, the Chaldeans of the Assyrians, the Druids of the Gauls, the Samanaei <note>likely referring to Buddhist or Indian monks</note> of the Bactrians, those of the Celts who practiced philosophy, and the Magi of the Persians."

<header>C. VITRINGA</header>

that they called all peoples outside their own region **barbarians** <margin>Chapter 88.</margin> <note>referring to a chapter in Plato's work or a cited commentary</note>, and that the interpretation of *Hesychius* <note>the 5th-century lexicographer</note> arose from this fact. This usage is very frequent in the writings of *Herodotus* <note>the famous 5th-century BC Greek historian</note> and other ancient authors, and the Apostle Paul seems to follow them in the *Epistle to the Romans*, chapter 1:14: *I am a debtor both to Greeks and to barbarians, both to the wise and to the foolish* <note>original Greek: Ἕλλησι καὶ βαρβάροις, σοφοῖς τε καὶ ἀνοήτοις ὀφειλέτης εἰμί</note>. In this instance, Paul seems to have interpreted "barbarian" as "foolish" <note>original Greek: βάρβαρον (*barbaron*) interpreted as ἀνόητον (*anoēton*)</note> based on the common way of speaking at that time.

There exists, however, another passage in *1 Corinthians 14:11* which greatly aids our explanation: *If then I do not know the meaning of the sound, I shall be a barbarian to the speaker, and the speaker a barbarian to me* <note>original Greek: Ἐὰν οὖν μὴ εἰδῶ τὴν δύναμιν τῆς φωνῆς, ἔσομαι τῷ λαλοῦντι βάρβαρος, καὶ ὁ λαλῶν ἐμοὶ βάρβαρος</note>. In Latin, this is: *If therefore I do not know the power of the voice, I shall be a barbarian to the one speaking, and the one speaking a barbarian to me* <note>original Latin: Si igitur non sciero vim vocis, ero loquenti barbarus, & loquens mihi barbarus</note>. This means it will seem to me that he is stuttering, and I will seem the same to him <note>original Latin: balbutire</note>.

In Dutch, this would be: *so he shall be barbarian to me* <note>original Dutch: soo sal hy my barbarisch sijn</note>. However, common usage has shifted so that we now think of this word as implying cruelty. Therefore, we might say it more clearly as: *so he shall seem to me to be babbling* <note>original Dutch: soo sal hy my schijnen te babbelen</note>. For we often think that when we do not understand others speaking, it should be blamed on a fault in their pronunciation.

When all these things are compared—with each other and with the nature of the matter itself—we believe that the word **confuse** <note>Hebrew: בלל (*balal*)</note> joined with the word **language** <note>Hebrew: שפה (*saphah* - literally "lip")</note> can signify such a confusion of human speech as one can see in those who are tongue-tied or stuttering. This confusion was so severe and harsh that people were unable to understand one another's speech. Eventually, the men involved in this plan <note>the building of the Tower of Babel</note>, fearing Divine vengeance and weary of the work they had begun, decided to seek other places to live. In this way, they were dispersed across the face of the entire world.

But if, by chance, this interpretation of the word **confuse** <note>Hebrew: בלל (*balal*)</note> should displease anyone because it is new and unusual, we can...

*But God, who is the severe Avenger of His own majesty and holiness, did not wish to tolerate this bold crime until its final completion. Instead, He Himself formed a plan for the ruin of that work, which this wicked crowd was promoting daily with its industry. "Until now," He said, "there has been only one speech heard in the world, one and the same concern for preserving the human race; until now, no disagreement has separated the minds of brothers, and no jealousy of power has inflamed them. But this work they are undertaking is too difficult and unjust. Therefore, let us subvert these ill-omened machinations and these most wicked plans; let us cast the fire of discord among them, so that each person acts according to what pleases himself, not what pleases others. Let each follow the guidance and opinion of his own mind rather than that of his brothers. Thus, when a disagreement of all their minds has arisen in this way, let them be scattered through the climates and regions of the whole world!"*

And indeed, we seem to find the remnants of this opinion even in the ancient writings of the Hebrews...

->These indeed then<-

*Jupiter, son of Saturn, hid in his anger:* <note>original Latin: *Iupiter Saturnius abscondit iratus:* Vitringa continues the quotation from Hesiod’s *Works and Days*, line 138.</note>
Truly, if Jupiter, son of Saturn <note>referring to the king of the gods, Zeus, whose father was Cronus/Saturn</note>, hid them from himself, they do not seem to have conversed further with his ministers and the rest of the blessed gods on earth. Instead, being cast down from the presence of Jupiter, they lived in the lower regions under the earth, which is why they were also called *subterranean* <note>Greek: ὑποχθόνιοι (*hypochthonioi*)</note>. This is all the more likely since it is certain that the fictions of the pagans reached that far, having been drawn from certain ancient narrations of the holy nation <note>the Jews</note>, some of which were even recorded in the Holy Bible. We have a passage in the *Second Epistle of Peter, chapter 2:4: God did not spare the angels who sinned, but casting them into Tartarus <note>term: Tartarus; the deepest abyss of the underworld</note>, delivered them into chains of darkness, to be kept for judgment.* <note>original Greek: ὁ Θεὸς ἀγγέλων ἁμαρτησάντων οὐκ ἐφείσατο, ἀλλὰ σειραῖς ζόφου ταρταρώσας παρέδωκεν εἰς κρίσιν τετηρημένους: Vitringa also provides the Latin: Deus Angelis qui peccaverunt, non pepercit, sed in tartarum detrusos catenis caliginis tradidit, iudicio asservatos.</note> There exists another in the *Epistle of Jude, verse 6: And the angels who did not keep their own origin, he has kept in eternal chains under* **DARKNESS** <note>original Greek: Αγγέλους τε τοὺς μὴ τηρήσαντας τὴν ἑαυτῶν ἀρχὴν δεσμοῖς ἀϊδίοις ὑπὸ ζόφον τετήρηκεν: Latin: Angelos verò qui non servarunt suam originem, vinculis æternis sub CALIGINE servavit.</note>. These descriptions seem to me to agree perfectly with what we just noted from *Hesiod*. Nor do I see any reason to despise the interpretation of that most learned man <note>Heinsius</note>, who understands the word *spirits* <note>Greek: δαίμονες (*daimones*)</note> to be implied with the word *second* <note>Greek: δεύτεροι (*deuteroi*)</note>. For these are indeed *spirits*, and the first race <note>the Golden Age</note> were also called *spirits*. However, if this grammatical structure is displeasing, why should we not join the Greek words in this way? *These indeed are called second rank blessed subterranean mortals* (which is to say, they *are* subterranean). In this case, every doubt is removed and the facts correspond to one another; for it is clear from *line 116* that the ancient beings were also mortals.

# CHAPTER II.

->*In which certain arguments are presented which demonstrate that all languages except Hebrew arose through the passage of time.*<-

Truly, we would have spent our efforts in vain in presenting our commentaries on the history written by Moses, had we not believed ourselves driven by certain reasonings to embrace that opinion which maintains that the diversity of languages and <term>idioms</term> <gloss>the specific way a language is used by a group</gloss> arose through the passage of time, and not at all during the aforementioned <term>Confusion of Languages</term> <gloss>the biblical event at the Tower of Babel where God reportedly dispersed humanity by changing their speech</gloss>. It is our intention to set forth some of these arguments in this chapter, in the order in which they first occur to us; for we shall make no selection or hierarchy here.

If we examine either the ancient or more recent commentaries of the Hebrews and Christians, we will find it established that nearly all of them have taught—based on the context of the sacred history—that this notorious deed <note>The rebellion at Babel.</note> is to be attributed primarily to the descendants of Ham, and perhaps also to some of the descendants of Japheth. However, they hold that the blessed Shem and his grandsons were preserved from this transgression through a singular care of the Almighty God, as they were the heirs of that blessing which Divine Mercy had assigned to them. <note>In biblical tradition, Noah’s three sons—Shem, Ham, and Japheth—represented the ancestors of all nations. Shem is the traditional ancestor of the Semitic peoples, including the Hebrews.</note>

Let us consider the discourse of <term>Flavius Josephus</term> <gloss>a first-century Jewish historian whose works are vital for understanding ancient Jewish perspectives</gloss>, which he established regarding the 10th chapter of Genesis in Book I of the *Antiquities of the Jews*, chapter 5:

<note>original Greek: Ἐξῆρε δ’ αὐτοὺς πρός τε ὕβριν τoῦ Θεοῦ καὶ κτ̃ [καταφρόνησιν] ναβρώδης. ὃς υἱωνὸς μεν̀ ὢν χάμου τoῦ νώχε, πληρὸς δ’ καὶ κτ̃</note>
*Nimrod incited them to such an insult and contempt of God. He was the grandson of Ham, the son of Noah, a man of daring and [great strength]...* <note>Vitringa cites Josephus to show that the rebellion was led by Nimrod, a descendant of Ham, further supporting the idea that Shem's lineage was not involved in the "Confusion."</note>

<note>Vitringa begins by quoting the Greek historian Flavius Josephus, who describes Nimrod's influence over the people.</note>
...the hand of women, he persuaded them not to attribute to God the source of their happiness, but to believe that their own virtue provided these things for them. He gradually changed the state of affairs into a **tyranny**, thinking that the only way to turn men away from the fear of God was to keep them continually dependent on his own power. He even threatened to take revenge on God if He should wish to flood the earth again; for he said he would build a tower higher than the water could reach. <note>original Greek: "χεῖρα γυναικῶν... ὕδωρ ἀναβαῖναι δυνηθείη." from Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, 1.4.2.</note>

Moreover, **Nimrod** (also called Nabrodes), who was the grandson of Ham and the great-grandson of Noah, incited them to this defiance and contempt for God. He was a bold man and a man of action, who repeatedly boasted that their present prosperity was owed not to God, but to their own courage. And so he gradually drew the matter toward a tyranny, believing that men would defect from God to himself if they relied on his protection. At the same time, he promised that he would bring them aid against God, should He want to flood the world again; for he would build a tower whose height the force of the waves would not be able to overcome. 

The <term>Jerusalem Paraphrase</term> <gloss>Also known as the Targum Yerushalmi, an ancient Aramaic translation and expansion of the Hebrew Bible</gloss> corresponds to the account of Flavius Josephus:

*He was a man powerful in hunting in sin before the Lord, because he hunted the children of men with their tongues <note>original Aramaic: "בלישנהון" (be-lishnehon); this suggests Nimrod used persuasive speech or the manipulation of language to lead people astray.</note> and said to them: "Recede from the judgments of God, and adhere to the laws of Nimrod."*

That same sentiment exists in that very ancient commentary called the <term>Yelammedenu</term> <gloss>A lost midrashic work, parts of which survive in later collections like the Midrash Tanchuma</gloss>:

Rabbi Aibu, in the name of Rabbi Jose the Galilean, says: In three places the inhabitants of the world divided themselves against the <term>Holy One, Blessed be He</term> <gloss>A standard Jewish title for God</gloss>: once in the days of the generation of the flood, once in the days of Gog and Magog <note>A biblical reference to a future apocalyptic conflict.</note>, and here at Babel, where it is said, "they said each to his neighbor," Cush to Put, and Put to Canaan. <note>original Hebrew: "כוש לפוט ופוט לכנען"; this refers to the alliances between the descendants of Ham.</note>

*“The words of **Moses** (he says) in Genesis 11:2, 3, 4: 'And it happened when they set out from the east'; these are not to be referred to all those discussed in chapter 10. But once you have found the truth, you will find it to be so fruitful that arguments for it will be suggested to you from every side—even the kind you did not seek before. We have brought Abraham’s most prudent servant <note>This refers to Eliezer of Damascus, mentioned in Genesis 15.</note> onto the stage, but he can certainly sustain a double persona here. We have said that he himself was a *Syrian*, and indeed originating from *Damascus*; however, we have not yet proved that those Damascene Syrians used the same Hebrew language, though we have proved it regarding the Phoenicians, who were neighbors to the Syrians—indeed, who were themselves called Syrians. 

But let us now prove this from the name of this servant, which we have said is Eliezer <note>original Hebrew: אלי עזר (*Eli-ezer*)</note>. Indeed, the name *Eliezer*, which was undoubtedly given to him in Syria at his birth according to the custom of all peoples, is clearly Hebrew, and it signifies: *My God is my help*, from *El* [God] and *Ezer* [help]. Because of this, the name later became very familiar to the nation of the Israelites. Since we can best judge the language of the ancients from the names given to regions or peoples—as these names were highly expressive <term>emphatica: names in the ancient world often functioned as descriptions of character or divine providence</term>—it will also be permitted for us to conclude from this *Syrian* name that the language of the Syrians at that time was the same as *Hebrew*. Clearly, those who said (and who, I ask, has almost not said it?) that the Hebrew language was preserved only in the family of *Heber* <note>Heber, or Eber, is the biblical ancestor from whom the name "Hebrew" is traditionally derived. But this servant has led us from Chaldea into Syria; let him lead us back again from Syria into Chaldea. All words are merely signs of things, and the things are what are signified. Is one person then more fortunate because they signify a thing through this word rather than that one? The **Hebrews** express that which we perceive through reason and bring forth with the mouth through *davar* <note>original Hebrew: דבר</note>; the **Greeks** through *logos* <note>original Greek: λόγον</note>; the **Latins** through *sermo*. ...those who were in charge of thousands, he says, were called "Chiliarchs" <note>original Greek: *Chiliarchos*, meaning a leader of a thousand men</note> by the Persians; and other narrow passes are called the "Susian Gates" <note>original: *Susidas Pylas*</note> by the Persians. Many examples of this kind occur throughout the works of historians. Eusebius says that certain serpents are called "good spirits" <note>original Greek: *agathous daimonas*</note> by the Phoenicians; Herodian tells us that Venus is called "Heavenly" <note>original Greek: *ouranian*</note> by the Africans. In Africa, the names Pithecusa and Ampelusia <note>Pithecusa likely refers to "Monkey Island" and Ampelusia to "Vineyard"</note> are names translated into Greek from the Punic language, as Diodorus witnesses in his twentieth book. Mela, in his first book, notes that what the Greeks call an *aspis* <term>aspis|A venomous snake, usually a cobra or viper</term>, the Latins call a *clupea*. Athenaeus, in his sixth book, says: "The Celts approach one another, even when at war, with companions whom they call 'parasites.'" That is, he calls them by a Gallic word which signifies "parasites" in Greek. The one whom Procopius calls *kyrton* <note>original Greek: *kyrton*, meaning "hunchback"</note> is called *Gibbus* by [Ammianus] Marcellinus. Even we, when writing in Latin, call a certain city in Brabant *Sylva Ducis* <note>Latin for "The Duke's Forest," known in Dutch as 's-Hertogenbosch</note>. Furthermore, the Greek translators of the sacred books <note>referring to the Septuagint, the Greek version of the Old Testament</note> set down not a few names of places in Greek, such as "oak" <note>original Greek: *drun*</note>, "high" <note>original Greek: *hypsēlēn*</note>, "acorn of mourning" <note>original Greek: *balanon penthous*</note>, "city of letters" <note>original Greek: *polin grammatōn*</note>, and "zagina." Thus far, Hugo Grotius.

But Grotius was not the only one who raised this doubt with such plausibility; he was certainly followed by the learned Pierre-Daniel Huet in that elegant work titled *Evangelical Demonstration*, Proposition IV, page 246. Huet produced not only more examples, but even stronger ones.

> To these, he says, I add the example of the translator of the Vulgate Scripture <note>St. Jerome, who translated the Bible into Latin</note>, who, in explaining that passage: "She shall be called Woman <note>original Hebrew: *Ishah*</note> because she was taken from Man <note>original Hebrew: *Ish*</note>"; expressed the same word-play using Latin names: "She shall be called *Virago*, because she was taken from *Vir* <note>Man</note>."

Alexander Polyhistor calls *Isaac*, whose name in Hebrew sounds like "laughter," by the Greek name *Gelota* <note>original Greek: *gelōta*, meaning laughter</note>. *Esau*, who was also named *Edom* (which means "Red" <note>original Latin: *Rufo*</note>), was called *Erythras* by the Greeks <note>from the Greek word for red</note>. *Og*, who was the King of Bashan and received that name from burning or cooking, was called *Typhon* by some Greeks—a word that carries the same meaning. He who [had] the name *Cephas* from Christ...

### I 2

The Israelites were oppressed by the Egyptians, as can be seen in <margin>Exodus 1</margin> Exodus 1. And so we have understood that the names of both the father and the brother of Moses are to be found from elsewhere, and were not transposed <note>translated or adapted into Hebrew</note> by Moses himself. I ask you again: for what reason would Moses have done this, when the names were of such a kind that posterity could have drawn lessons of teaching from them? Is it not very likely that a historian, dedicated to translating names, would equally translate the names of his parent and his brother—indeed, would translate them even more than the names of others? Surely this would pertain to that piety <note>filial duty and respect</note> which he owed to his parent and his family. 

And yet we see that Moses the historian acted otherwise, if the opinion of these famous men <note>likely referring to contemporary 17th-century biblical critics who argued Moses translated names for his audience</note> is to be accepted. Moreover, why would he translate the name of his mother more than that of his father, or why would he give us his own name as a sign <note>a symbolic explanation of its meaning</note> rather than his brother's? Truly, one must judge either that Moses wrote his history without reason, if the conjecture of these men is valid; or that this conjecture is weak, and that Moses recorded the names just as they were received among those nations at that time.

But other things must be considered which we have observed in this matter, and conclusions must be drawn from them. We think that what is reported to us in Book 1, Chapter 14, verses 7 and 8, is most relevant to the present case:

Another argument of no less weight presents itself. There is almost no famous man among those who have excelled others in the knowledge of divine and human affairs who has not sought those most ancient names—whether of persons or of places found in the writings of the Gentiles—from the Sacred Scriptures. ...race, mortals were gradually dispersed into scattered places and regions. While living there, they explained their origins to their children, and according to the simplicity of that age, perhaps expressed them through certain signs. The children, in turn, did the same for future posterity. Now, it is indeed certain that men are more prone to superstition the more ignorant and dull—or rather, simple—they are. Since nothing was established for them concerning the origins of things, except for that which their parents had handed down to them, they began to regard as a <term>Deity <note>original: "Numine"</note></term>, and later to worship and venerate, the one whom their parents had taught them was the first of their race. 

Hence come those names of *Ammon*, *Japheth*, and others. Although it should be known that among some groups these traditions were lesser, while among others they were greater, more numerous, and more esteemed. Now we proceed, and we say that those Princes and Parents of nations handed down to their posterity the names of their own parents unchanged, since they learned those same names from their own parents along with the very language from which those names were composed. Therefore, they taught their sons the names of their parents exactly as they were, without any or even the slightest change. 

Since this was done in such a way, it must be that Moses did the same, because the names related by Moses agree with those pagan names as accurately as possible. If, therefore, those names were handed down unchanged which can be drawn from the monuments of the Nations, then those which exist in the records of Moses will certainly be unchanged as well; otherwise, they would have been as different from each other as possible. From this we conclude either that Moses did not change proper names, or that the names of *Vulcan*, *Ham*, *Japheth*, and others are not to be referred to those which Moses recorded—which latter point, however...

<meta>This page continues Vitringa’s argument that ancient writers preserved the original names of people and places as they were used in their own eras. ->### C. VITRINGA<-

In this matter, we believe that no historians have been brought onto the stage who changed all names—not even many—and only a few who transposed certain ones. For it is altogether certain and beyond doubt that the most ancient of historians record the names of persons and places exactly as they were used by the people of that time. It would be a task of immense labor to demonstrate this from every individual case, since every single page would provide enough evidence for separate arguments. Let us merely note one or two passages from *Herodotus* <note>Herodotus (c. 484–425 BC), often called the "Father of History," was a Greek writer who recorded the traditions and geography of the ancient world.</note>, who stands above the rest in antiquity. Thus he writes in *Book II, page 110*: *In that city (Busiris) is the largest temple of Isis, situated in the very middle of the Egyptian Delta.* Now, *Isis* is the one who in the Greek language is called Demeter <note>original Greek: Δημήτηρ</note>. *Page 121:* The Egyptians who live in the marshlands use an ointment which the Egyptians call *Kiki* <note>original: KIKI; a type of castor oil used for lamps and anointing.</note>. *Page 122:* *Thus, when the gate is set against the force of the water, it immediately moves and draws the* *Baris* <note>original: BARIM; a specific type of Egyptian flat-bottomed boat.</note>. *For this is the name for these vessels.* *Page 142:* Later, *Sennacherib* <note>original Hebrew: סנחריב (Sanheriv)</note>, King of the Arabs and Assyrians. *Page 143:* *Piromis born from a long line of Piromis.* However, a *Piromis* in the Greek language is a "gentleman" <note>original Greek: καλὸς κἀγαθὸς, literally 'the beautiful and the good,' referring to an ideal of noble character.</note>. And a little later: *And that finally Horus, the son of Osiris, whom the Greeks call Apollo, reigned there.* Now, *Osiris* in the Greek language is *Dionysus*, that is, Liber <note>Liber was the Roman god of wine and fertility, identified with the Greek Dionysus.</note>. *Page 147:* He built the court for *Apis*. *But Apis in the Greek language is Epaphus.* So too *Ashdod* <note>original Hebrew: אשדוד</note> occurs on *page 149*: *This is Azotos, which sustained the longest siege of all cities.*

<margin>2 Kings 23:29.</margin>
*Pharaoh Necho* <note>original Hebrew: פרעה נכה (Par'oh Nekoh)</note>. *In the same place: In the digging of which, under King* NECO, *one hundred and twenty thousand Egyptians perished.* You see how clear the evidence we have produced is from a very brief survey of that ancient historian's words: and we could produce infinitely more such examples.

# C. VITRINGA

Are not all these [names] Hebrew and composed according to Hebrew inflection? And by what reasoning could it have happened that Job, an Arab, would have given Hebrew names to his daughters if he had been using the Arabic dialect? Indeed, I cannot conclude anything else from this than that the Arabic dialect at that time was not much different from Hebrew. This is the single truth that we intend to prove with this evidence of ours.

However, I can easily guess what those who do not deign to embrace our opinion will object to this proposition: namely, that these names were transposed into the Hebrew language in the same way that we previously advised that the entire volume of **Job** was translated. It is possible that the same thing can be expressed by different words within the same language. This is especially true if we pay attention to the changeability and fluidity of human affairs, and most particularly of the **human language** <note>original: "Lingua humana"</note> through which those affairs are expressed. But these matters must be considered further.

We believe, therefore, in the first place, that nothing has ever given such an occasion for the origin of multiple languages as the **dispersion of the Eastern nations** <note>original: "dispersionem gentium Orientalium"</note> from the East into other regions. Hence, those who first withdrew from the East were the first to be subjected to a change in their language. The peoples who retreated further and were scattered into more distant lands saw their idiom more greatly changed than those who sought homes nearby. Indeed, many things pertaining to the change of languages—and the very reason for that change—can be very easily deduced from this fact. We shall attempt to explain this matter, as it is a most worthy subject.

If we turn our attention to our **first Parents** <note>Adam and Eve and their immediate descendants</note>, who lived before the **Flood** <note>original: "inundationem orbis," literally "the inundation of the world."</note>, we will not wonder greatly that they constantly cultivated and preserved their language, since almost everything that usually induces a change in language was absent from them. We do not find that they were dispersed from the East into other regions; for this is not clear from the **Sacred Scripture** <note>original: "Codice sacro," literally "the Sacred Code."</note>. No established dominions were settled among them by which the minds of men are alienated. For among them there was no...

## C. VITRINGA
### SACRED OBSERVATIONS

...between those groups there was no distinction, except that which proceeded from piety toward God, whence some seem to have been called <term>Sons of God: בני אלהים (B’nei Elohim)</term> and others <term>Sons of Men: בני אדם (B’nei Adam)</term>. <note>Vitringa refers to the two lineages mentioned in Genesis—the descendants of Seth and the descendants of Cain—suggesting that despite their moral differences, they still spoke the same language.</note> Without a doubt, they engaged in mutual trade, and by these means human society was strengthened. If we observe all these things, by what reasoning could it happen that their languages would have undergone a change? 

But another factor was added, which is by far the greatest: namely, the **longevity** <term>longaevitas: the remarkably long lifespans</term> of those men who preceded that universal flood. A very few generations were able to reach two thousand years. <note>In the biblical chronology Vitringa follows, the long lives of figures like Methuselah meant that fewer "links" were needed to pass down speech, preventing the natural "drift" seen in modern languages.</note> And from this it happened that they constantly retained one and the same language before the flood; for they themselves did not become the authors of changing the language, nor did others arise to do so. 

Moreover, the holy **Noah** passed on this same idiom to his descendants, who also used it in the first centuries. For they themselves wished to take care that they would not be scattered. But the opposite occurred; for that God, whom they had violently offended by the construction of the City and the **Tower of Babel** <note>original: "turris Babylonicae"</note>, scattered them. From that age, the human race was dispersed; but not immediately into the most remote and far-off regions. 

Indeed, the East was sufficient to contain those few bands of men—or rather, families—even though they were distinct. This is confirmed by the entire sacred context written by **Moses**, not to mention the traditions of other nations. Reason also suggests the same. What cause would the men of that age have had to separate themselves from other men—who were quite few in number—and to seek out foreign fields, when the greater part of the East lay open to them, pleas- <note>The original Latin text "amae-" likely completes as "amaena," meaning pleasant or lovely.</note>
