Let us, however, bring forward to illustrate this opinion that passage which is found in the fifth book of Moses <note>Deuteronomy 11:1</note>: **"And you shall love the LORD your God and keep His charge, His statutes, His judgments, and His commandments always"** <note>original Hebrew: ואהבת את יהוה אלהיך ושמרת משמרתו וחקתיו ומשפטיו ומצותיו כל הימים</note>: *And you shall love Jehovah your God and observe His observation, and His* **decrees** <note>original Greek: δόγματα (*dogmata*)</note>, *and His judgments, and His precepts through all your days.* It is quite manifest that these words look back to the Law given to the descendants of Abraham <note>original Latin: Abrahamidis</note> as promulgated by God. Anyone may encounter many similar testimonies. 

Let us add only a little regarding the true meaning of the word **charge** <note>original Hebrew: משמרת (*mishmeret*), often translated as "watch," "guard," or "service"</note>, which seems to us to be taken from the office of the Levites and Priests. Indeed, the Priests and Levites were considered as soldiers in the Old Instrument <note>The Old Testament</note>, which is why terms like *station, guard-duty, encampment*, and similar duties proper to soldiers are attributed to them. Let us compare the remarkable passage found in the third book <note>Leviticus 8:35</note>: *“And you shall remain at the door of the tent of meeting day and night for seven days, and you shall keep the* **charge of the LORD** <note>original Hebrew: משמרת יהוה (*mishmeret Yehovah*)</note>, *the watch of Jehovah, so that you do not die.”* This is exactly as it is written in Habakkuk, chapter 2, verse 1: **"I will stand upon my watch"** <note>original Hebrew: על משמרתי אעמדה (*al mishmarti emodah*)</note>: *I stood upon my guard.* It happened, therefore, because of this status of the Levites and Priests, that all mortals who excelled in piety were thereafter said to *observe the* **charge of the LORD**, which we believe is exactly what happened in this passage. From this, therefore, that which we warned of before is clearly gathered.

Indeed, let us add a passage on the same subject from the first book <note>Genesis 32:1–2</note>: **"And Jacob went on his way, and the messengers of God met him. And when Jacob saw them, he said: This is the camp of God"** <note>original Hebrew: ויעקב הלך לדרכו ויפגעו בו מלאכי אלהים: ויאמר יעקוב כאשר ראם מחנה אלהים זה</note>: *And Jacob proceeded on his way, and the Angels of God met him. And Jacob said, when he had noticed them:*

*It is an Army of Angels.* For I believe this passage should be translated in this way, and that in this place by **Elohim** <note>original Hebrew: אלהים; usually translated as "God" or "gods"</note> one should understand **Angels**, not **God**. I judge this to be clear enough from the preceding text, where this *Army of Elohim* <note>original Hebrew: מחנה אלהים (*machane elohim*)</note> is called the *Angels of God* <note>original Hebrew: מלאכי אלהים (*malache elohim*)</note>. Perhaps no one would be surprised if I translated **Elohim** as **Angels** in another book of the **Holy Scriptures**, since the **Apostles** themselves do so several times; but to do this in the first book of **Moses** <note>The Book of Genesis</note> will perhaps seem foreign or strange, because **Angels** seem to have only formally acquired that name during the full implementation of the **Old Testament** era. But if anyone wishes to think of it this way, they might consider that in this first book of **Moses**, modes of speaking are sometimes employed which only became established in subsequent times—a point we have just noted. If anyone doubts this, behold the phrase **as angels** <note>original Greek: ὡς ἄγγελοι (*hos angeloi*)</note>, which is found in this same volume, chapter III, verse 5. There, the discourse is recounted which the **Serpent** had with **Eve**, and among his arguments this is held:

> *For God knows that on the day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened and you will be,* <note>original Hebrew: כאלחים יודעי טוב ורע (*k'elohim yode'e tov va-ra*)</note> *as gods, knowing good and evil.*

*That is, as Angels.* Why? Would a sound mind, such as we perceive that of our mother **Eve** to have been, think that she could become equal to **God her Creator**? Would the serpent, intending to deceive the woman, take an argument from a ridiculous and impossible thing? To me, indeed, it does not seem likely. If anyone thinks otherwise, however, he may enjoy his own judgment.

Moreover, **Jehovah said to Moses: "When you go back to return to Egypt, see that you perform before Pharaoh all those wonders which I have put in your hand."** <note>Original Latin: "autem Iehova Mosi, cum vadas Tu ad revertendum in Aegyptum, vide, omnia illa prodigia, quæ posui in manu tua, facias coram Pharaone." Namely, **Josephus the Historian** <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Jewish-Roman historian.</note>, in the first book of his work *Against Apion the Alexandrian*—a work written with truly great erudition and careful research, in which he proves the antiquity of his nation using foreign writers while simultaneously refuting the errors and slanders of those same authors—frequently mentions that many ancient historians record in their accounts that **Moses was infected with leprosy**, and that the entire population was also seized by ulcers or some other kind of disease. Let us recall the actual opinion of those men in the words that are read today in **Josephus**. Indeed, **Lysimachus** <note>An ancient Greek historian whose work is now lost, except for fragments preserved by Josephus.</note> relates:

"In the time of Bocchoris <note>A legendary or semi-historical King of Egypt, often identified with Bakenranef (8th century BCE), though here associated with the era of the Exodus.</note>, King of the Egyptians, the Jewish people, being lepers and scabby and suffering from certain other diseases, took refuge in the temples to beg for food. Because so many people had fallen into illness, a famine occurred in Egypt. Bocchoris, the King of the Egyptians..." <note>Original Greek: "Ἐπὶ Βοκχόρεως τῶν Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέως, τὸν λαὸν τῶν ἰουδαίων λεπρὸς ὄντας καὶ ψωρὸς καὶ ἄλλα νοσήματά τινα ἔχοντας, εἰς τὰ ἱερὰ καταφεύγοντας μεταιτεῖν τροφήν. παμπόλλων δὲ ἀνθρώπων νοσηλία περιπεσόντων ἀκαρπίαν ἐν τῇ ἀγύπτῳ γενέσθαι. Βόκχοριν δὲ τὸν τῶν Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέα."</note>

**When Bocchoris was ruling the Egyptians, the Jewish people, infected with leprosy, scabies, and certain other diseases, fled to the temples for the sake of begging for food. Because of this, as many men were seized by diseases, a period of sterility arose in Egypt. Bocchoris, therefore, King of the Egyptians,** and so forth. <note>Vitringa provides a Latin translation of the Greek quote: "Aegyptiis imperante Bocchori populum Iudæorum lepra, scabie, & aliis quibusdam morbis infectum ad templa confugisse cibum mendicandi gratiâ. Quare cum fieret, ut multi homines morbis corriperentur, sterilitatem in Aegypto extitisse. Bocchorin igitur Aegyptiorum Regem."</note> But the **Egyptian** writers especially handed down this tradition about **Moses**, insisting that the man was a **leper**, even though they are otherwise not stingy in describing his virtues. That learned writer <note>Josephus</note> says against the words of **Manetho** <note>An Egyptian priest and historian (3rd century BCE) whose work is a primary source for Egyptian chronology, though it contains polemics against the Jews.</note>, which he had previously cited: *It remains for me to speak against him concerning Moses. The Egyptians consider this man to be wonderful and divine, but they try to claim him for themselves with unbelievable blasphemy, saying that he was a citizen of the City of the Sun <note>Heliopolis, one of the oldest cities in ancient Egypt and a center for the worship of the sun god Ra.</note>, and indeed one of the priests of that same place, who was driven out together with the others because of leprosy.* <note>Original Greek: λοιπὸν μοὶ πρὸς αὐτὸν εἰπεῖν περὶ Μωϋσέως τοῦτον δὲ τὸν ἄνδρα θαυμαστὸν μὲν ᾿Αιγύπτιοι καὶ θεῖον νομίζουσι... Original Latin: Restat contra ipsum disceptem de Mose. Mirabilem equidem & Divinum fuisse hunc hominem existimant Ægyptii...</note>

I can indeed grant to our Josephus that these historians, not having a clear view of all those most ancient matters and being busy proclaiming the glory of their own nation—that is, the Egyptian nation—added certain things either from conjecture or the rumors of that time (which were, without a doubt, held in contempt of the Jews) which do not correspond to the truth. Yet, I do not believe this entire story was fabricated by them out of pure malice. For their writings breathe a certain simplicity and integrity. 

For this reason, I would believe that there existed certain records in the monuments of that time, from which they did not so much invent such details out of malice as they inferred them from a simple desire for the glory of their own people. Not to mention, it is possible that everything was not recorded in those ancient monuments (from which they transcribed their histories) with total accuracy regarding the truth of the events as they happened. Indeed, it is highly probable that the Egyptians, burning with the greatest hatred toward the Jews, either failed to pass down the events to their posterity in this way, or even recorded them in the public acts—

...as was fitting, but from certain minor circumstances they constructed a story of this kind that would bring the Hebrew people into contempt. I certainly believe that the action of Moses narrated in this place <note>Vitringa is likely referring to Exodus 4:6, where Moses’s hand becomes leprous as a sign from God, or perhaps the broader context of the plagues.</note> provided the occasion for the opinion of those men just mentioned regarding *Moses the leper*. From these, they were later able to seize the opportunity to defame the Jewish people.

In the following centuries, the very writings of Moses seem to have nourished this opinion of theirs. For we notice that very many precepts handed down by Moses in those books concern leprous men, their cleansing, and other related matters. They <note>The Egyptian historians and critics of the Jews.</note> believed these laws referred to leprosy and other diseases <note>original Greek: νοσήματα (*nosemata*), meaning sicknesses or plagues.</note> with which that entire people was infected when they departed from Egypt. 

It is also not entirely improbable that poor, needy, and oppressed men—as the Jews were in Egypt—were more vulnerable to those types of diseases than the rest of the Egyptians, who looked after their own bodies more sumptuously and delicately. Perhaps this also relates to what is written in this same book <note>Exodus</note>, chapter 15, verse 26, where God speaks thus: <note>original Hebrew: כל המחלה אשר שמתי במצרים לא אשים עליך כי אני יהוה רפאך</note> *Every disease with which I afflicted Egypt, I will not put upon you, for I am Jehovah* YOUR HEALER. While these final words are taken in this context to mean that God would turn away every disease from them, they could have been understood by others as if the people had already been seized by disease, for which God provided a cure.

### SACRED OBSERVATIONS. 225

2 Samuel 1:18 <note>Though the text cites verse 18, the Hebrew quoted is actually verse 19: "The glory of Israel is slain upon your high places."</note> <note>original Hebrew: הַצְּבִי יִשְׂרָאֵל עַל בָּמוֹתֶיךָ חָלָל</note> Junius and Tremellius <note>Francis Junius and Immanuel Tremellius were 16th-century scholars famous for their Latin translation of the Bible.</note> translate this as: *O glory of Israel, pierced upon your heights.* The Dutch <note>original Latin: Belgæ</note> translate it: **O ornament of Israel / on your heights he is slain.** Without a doubt, they have imitated the Hebrew interpreters, who took that letter *He* [ה] as a "call" <note>original Hebrew: הַקְּרִיאָה (*ha-kri'ah*)</note>; that is, as a <term>vocative</term> <note>The grammatical case used when addressing someone directly, like saying "O, Glory!"</note>. But for what reason, I ask, have they made these words obscure—words which no translator could find easier to rearrange? For by approving of this <term>self-will</term> <note>original Greek: αὐθαδείᾳ (*authadeia*), implying a stubborn or bold interpretative choice</note>, they trouble themselves with many useless and unnecessary petty questions; namely, who is to be understood here as the "glory of Israel"? Is it God? Is it the land of Canaan? They could have very easily abstained from these questions if they had followed the simplest word arrangement. 

But was this done by them because of the *Zakef* <note>A Hebrew cantillation mark or "accent" that acts as a comma or semi-colon.</note> accent which is on the word *Israel*, and which seems to indicate a division? Truly, I would not believe so. For if any translator wishes to account for every one of those tiniest accents, he will deceive both himself and others six hundred times in explaining the scriptures. For those marks are arranged as much for chanting as they are for the distinction of sentences. 

Instead, they seem to have embraced this interpretation because of the suffix attached to the word *after* <note>Vitringa appears to be discussing the grammatical relationship of the preposition.</note> which is found in the word *your high places* <note>original Hebrew: בָּמוֹתֶיךָ (*bamotekha*)</note>. It did not seem possible to refer this "your" to anything other than the "glory of Israel," because nothing else had preceded it. Therefore, if that were certain, the phrase "glory of Israel" would absolutely have to be explained as a vocative. This logic certainly follows, even though it is very evident to us that the suffix "your" [ךָ] should not be referred back to the "glory of Israel." To make this manifest to others, I will first translate these words according to my own opinion, and then I will illustrate them. My version:

In this place David begins his lament in this way: *That glory of Israel is prostrated upon your high places*; he had his mind fixed on the mountainous region of Gilboa, in which these heroes had been laid low. But lest I seem to wish to be believed on my own word, let us examine verse 21, which proceeds as follows: <note>original Hebrew: הרי הגלבע אל טל ואל מטר עליכם (*Harei ha-Gilboa al tal ve-al matar aleichem*)</note> *O mountains of Gilboa, let there be neither dew nor rain upon you!* Here again the expression is <term>defective</term> <note>a grammatical term for a sentence where a word is omitted for poetic or emotional effect</note>, and the word <note>original Hebrew: יפול (*yipol*), meaning "falls"</note> "falls" is swallowed up by the laments and sighs, which the elegance of this song requires. 

But perhaps someone will think this passage is rather contrary to our opinion, because if David had respect to the <note>original Hebrew: הרי הגלבע (*Harei ha-Gilboa*)</note> *Mountains of Gilboa*, he should have said <note>original Hebrew: במותיכם (*bamoteichem*)</note> *in your* [plural] *high places* and not <note>original Hebrew: במותיך (*bamoteicha*)</note> *in your* [singular] *high places*, as we see it written now. Yet we ourselves wanted to raise this doubt for the very purpose of showing that its solution is extremely easy.

Undoubtedly, that which is said here as *Mountains of Gilboa* is to be explained as the mountainous region of Gilboa. In Dutch: <note>original Dutch: Het geberchte van Gilboa</note> *The mountain range of Gilboa*. To show that this corresponds to the truth, let us turn to the description of the event itself, which is found in the first book of *Samuel*, chapter 31:8. *And it happened the next day, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, they found Saul and his three sons* <note>original Hebrew: בהר הגלבע נופלים (*be-har ha-Gilboa noplim*)</note> *prostrate on the mountain (the mountainous region) of Gilboa*. There the Dutch themselves translate the Hebrew word for "mountain" <note>original Hebrew: הר (*har*)</note> as *mountain range* <note>original Dutch: geberchte</note>. From this, therefore, the doubt is plainly removed.

But, lest the smallest scrap of hesitation remain for anyone, we will add in confirmation of our transposition a <term>parallel</term> <note>original Greek: παράλληλον (*parallēlon*), referring to a matching or corresponding text</note> passage from verse 26 of this same chapter, where these same words are found: *How have the fallen...*

11. **2 Samuel 6:2.** *And David arose and went with all the people who were with him from Baal-Judah, to bring up from there the Ark of God* <note>original Hebrew: את ארון האלהים אשר נקרא שם שם יהוה צבאות יושב הכרובים עליו (*et aron ha-Elohim asher nikra shem shem YHWH Tzevaot yoshev ha-keruvim alav*)</note> | Junius and Tremellius <note>16th-century scholars known for their influential Latin translation of the Old Testament</note> translate it as: *To which is invoked the Name, the name of Jehovah of Hosts sitting on the Cherubim.* At first glance, this seems plausible. ...they had reached this understanding, but rather they could not extricate themselves from those difficulties which pressed upon them from every side, and hence they chose this version over others that seemed even more inconvenient. *Ludovicus de Dieu* <note>a 17th-century Dutch orientalist and theologian</note>, who understood the nature of the Hebrew language better than almost any other man, and whom we admire as often as we read him, certainly demonstrated the greatest acumen in this passage; however, he did not grasp the reality of the matter. This is something we may say freely. We shall report his opinion. Namely, first he praises *Junius* <note>Franciscus Junius, the elder, a famous 16th-century Hebraist</note> because he referred the word *alav* <term>עליו</term> <note>meaning "upon it"</note>, which is in the final part of the verse, back to *asher* <term>אשר</term> <note>the relative pronoun "which" or "that"</note>. But truly, this interpretation is opposed both to the grammatical construction of the words and to the very nature of the language. For if the word <term>עליו</term> (*alav*) belonged to <term>אשר</term> (*asher*), should it not have been written <term>אשר נקרא עליו</term> <note>original: *asher nikra alav*, "which is called upon it"</note>? Why would that <term>עליו</term> be found at the end of the verse after words that are very distinct from the preceding ones? Should not relative suffixes be referred to the immediately preceding nouns, provided nothing stands in the way? But indeed, nothing at all stands in the way here, as even the supporters of this opinion admit. All these things are so evident to those who are imbued with the knowledge of this language that they could not be more evident. But it is not even this way. This phrase <term>Φράסις</term> <note>original Greek: *phrasis*, meaning "expression" or "phrase"</note> <term>אשר נקרא עליו שם</term> <note>original Hebrew: *asher nikra alav shem*, "on which a name is called"</note> means something entirely different among the Hebrews. Let us consult a single parallel passage <term>παράλληλον</term> <note>original Greek: *parallēlon*</note>, and this matter will become manifest. It is found in the fifth book of Moses <note>Deuteronomy</note>, chapter 28, verse 10:

The Dutch Translators <note>the authors of the 1637 Dutch Authorized Version, the *Statenvertaling*</note> say best in the margin: **That you are named after the name of the Lord.** And they direct that a comparison be made between this passage and another, which is in Book 1 <note>Genesis</note>, chapter 48, verses 6 and 16, which is clearly brought in line with our own view. For in this case, neither the *begetting*, the *preservation* of the name, its transfer to others, its numbering, and the other things included in this "bearing" <note>original Greek: φερειν (*pherein*), meaning to bear or carry a name</note>, hold true in any sense. But what kind of *interpretation* <note>original Greek: εξηγησις (*exegesis*)</note> is this? Even if I were to grant that He [the Ark or God] is called *the Name* (which I do not grant, as I believe this was wrongly fabricated by the Jews from certain passages of Holy Scripture according to their own particular style), could any man understand how He could be called the *Name of Jehovah of Hosts*? Can God be called the *Name of God*? Can a man named John be called the *Name of John*? And yet, this most erudite man so entangled himself just so he could rearrange the Hebrew words "correctly." Regarding the integrity of the word **ka’ari** <note>original Hebrew: כארי. This is a famous crux in Psalm 22. The Masoretic text reads "like a lion," while many ancient versions and Christian commentators suggest a verb meaning "they pierced."</note>. To be sure, this most learned man insisted in that discourse that the word **ka’ari** <note>original Greek: τὸ כארי</note> is a present participle in the <term>Kal<note>The most basic grammatical form or "stem" of a Hebrew verb.</note></term> stem from the unused root **kur** <note>original Hebrew: כור</note>; and he proved that **ka’ari** was written in place of **ka’arim** <note>original Hebrew: כארים</note>, something that has also happened in very many other words. 

But although that excellent man carried out all those things of his with great erudition, he did not, however, investigate the reason why it happened that the last letter **Mem** <note>original Hebrew: ם</note> was omitted, and the letter **Aleph** <note>original Hebrew: א</note> was inserted between the **Kaph** <note>original Hebrew: כ</note> and the **Resh** <note>original Hebrew: ר</note>. We have therefore deemed it worthwhile to add our own thoughts on this matter at present, especially because we know of no others who have paid attention to it.

Therefore, the sequence of events must be traced from a little further back. Those <term>vowel points<note>Known as *niqqud*, these are the dots and dashes added to the Hebrew consonantal text to indicate vowel sounds.</note></term> which we see marked under our letters today were invented by the more diligent Jews for this reason: so that the true method of reading the scripture might be preserved and handed down to their distant descendants. 

For when they saw the Temple destroyed—the common monument and refuge, as it were, of their race—and saw their sacred things also perishing, the study of Scripture being neglected, and noticed that they themselves were for the most part cast out from the land once given to them by God as an inheritance, they nevertheless applied themselves with all zeal and industry to ensure that the Holy Scripture should remain untainted and be read by their posterity. I have no doubt that every man of sounder judgment will grant me this. Indeed, this has been established with such clear reasoning by the most excellent men of every kind in our century, that whoever thinks the contrary betrays either stubbornness or ignorance, no matter who he may be. 

Yet, while we maintain that the vowel points were added after the time of Christ, I would not want anyone to think that the Jews had nothing at all before then <note>Vitringa is entering the "Great Vowel Point Controversy," a major scholarly debate of the 17th century about whether the Hebrew vowels were divinely inspired and ancient, or a later human invention by the Masoretes.</note>...

...which might have compensated for their value in some way. For it is most certain to me that they wrote at least their common <term>Codices<note>Handwritten books or manuscripts.</note></term> in the same way that Rabbis are accustomed to record their writings today—that is, they used the letters **Aleph**, **Waw**, and **Yod** <note>original Hebrew: אוי</note> in place of vowels. Thus, the **Aleph** <note>original Hebrew: א</note> expressed the vowels *a* and *e*, the **Waw** <note>original Hebrew: ו</note> expressed *o* and *u*, and finally the **Yod** <note>original Hebrew: י</note> expressed the sound *i*, just as was done by other Eastern peoples. 

When, however, <term>vowel points<note>The system of dots and dashes (niqqud) added to the Hebrew text to indicate pronunciation.</note></term> were later substituted, since they were far more certain and clear, it happened that these letters—**Aleph**, **Waw**, and **Yod**—were removed from the words as being unnecessary and redundant. This could indeed be done correctly, because they were compensated for by the vowel points. Yet this could not be done with such exactness that no traces remained, from which it can be most clearly proven by us today that this was indeed done by them. And since this is the true conviction of our mind, it must be illustrated with a very few examples.

Let us therefore note the passage in *Hosea, chapter 10, verse 14*: **And a tumult shall arise among your people** <note>original Hebrew: וקאם שאון בעמיך (v’qam sha’on b’ameka)</note>. We notice here that the present participle from the root **qum** <note>original Hebrew: קום (to rise)</note> is written here as **qa’am** <note>original Hebrew: קאם</note>, when it ought to have been written as **qam** <note>original Hebrew: קם</note>. What, I ask, is the reason for this spelling? Certainly no other than what we have just given: that the Ancients, since vowel points had not yet been invented, used the letter **Aleph** <note>original Hebrew: א</note> in the Bible for the vowel <term>Kamets<note>A Hebrew vowel mark representing a long "a" sound.</note></term>, and that they therefore wrote **qa’am** <note>original Hebrew: קאם</note> for what we write as **qam** <note>original Hebrew: קם</note>. This letter **Aleph** <note>original Hebrew: א</note> was left here through an <term>error<note>original Greek: ἀκυρίαν (akyrian), meaning an impropriety or lack of precision in usage.</note></term> by the first <term>punctuators<note>The Masoretic scholars who standardized the Hebrew text and added vowel signs.</note></term>, which later scholars did not venture to remove. 

A similar reason exists for the superfluous letter **Aleph** <note>original Hebrew: א</note> in the words **ra’amah** <note>original Hebrew: ראמה</note> instead of **ramah** <note>original Hebrew: רמה (heights)</note>, and **ra’amot** <note>original Hebrew: ראמות</note> for **ramot** <note>original Hebrew: רמות (corals or heights)</note>, and **ha-sha’atim** <note>original Hebrew: השאטים (those who despise)</note> in *Ezekiel 28:24*, and...

# SACRED OBSERVATIONS

"In those days the Lord began to cut off parts of Israel" <note>original Hebrew: לקצות בישראל (*liktzot be-Yisrael*); this refers to 2 Kings 10:32.</note>. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> uses the term *to cut to pieces* <note>original Greek: συγκόπτειν (*synkoptein*)</note>. The Dutch <note>The *Statenvertaling*, the standard Dutch Bible translation of Vitringa's era.</note> translate this as **to shorten** or **cut down**, but in the margin they provide: **to cut off**. In my judgment, because the Hebrew text says *liktzot be-Yisrael*, we might not inappropriately say in Dutch: **to prune away at Israel** <note>original Dutch: *Israel te besnoepen*. The word implies trimming or nibbling away at the edges of a territory.</note>. Furthermore, the word *katzah* <note>meaning "to cut off" or "an end"</note> differs very little indeed from the meaning of the root *katzatz* <note>meaning "to chop off" or "sever"</note>.

***

**Isaiah 7:9:** "If you will not believe, surely you shall not be established" <note>original Hebrew: אם לא תאמינו כי לא תאמנו (*Im lo ta’aminu ki lo te’amenu*)</note>. The translators Junius and Tremellius <note>Authors of a famous 16th-century Latin Bible translation.</note> render this as: *Do you not believe? Because you are not established.* The Dutch say: **If you people do not believe, surely you shall not be established.** Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a prominent Dutch theologian and colleague of Vitringa.</note> translates: *Even if you do not believe, because you will not endure.* None of these versions should be dismissed. However, we add that these words can also be translated in this way: *Certainly you do not believe, because you are not established.* **Surely you do not believe, because you are not established.** <note>original Dutch: *Seeckerlijck ghy en gelooft niet / omdat ghy niet bevestigt zijt.*</note>

For the particle *im* <note>Usually translated as "if."</note> is sometimes taken to mean *certainly* or *surely* in the books of the Old Testament. I remember that I have often observed this in the annotations of that most elegant man, **Ludovicus de Dieu** <note>A renowned Dutch orientalist and linguist (1590–1642).</note>. I will add one or two proofs. It is found in Jeremiah 31:20: "Is Ephraim a precious son to me? *Certainly* a child of delights" <note>original Hebrew: אם ילד שעשועים (*im yeled sha’ashuim*)</note>. Similarly, in the Song of David <note>The Psalms.</note> 139:18: "*Certainly* you will slay the wicked, O God." <note>This citation is verse 19 in modern Bibles.</note> And the same is taught by **Kimchi** <note>David Kimchi, also known as Radak (c. 1160–1235), a highly influential medieval Jewish grammarian and commentator.</note> in his *Book of Roots*, where he adds many other examples, although we are not unaware that many of these are understood in different ways by other most learned men.

However, there can be no doubt that when these words are accepted in this sense, they produce a meaning that is both easy and suitable. It is clear that the kings of Syria and Israel, with their forces joined, had decreed not only to attack the land of Judah, but—

...to capture Jerusalem, to subject it to themselves, and to despoil *Ahaz* <note>original: *Achasum*</note> of his kingdom. And certainly, if the external condition of *Judah* and the whole kingdom were considered, it seemed entirely likely that the outcome would correspond to the enemies' expectations. For the land of *Judah* at that time was quite weak and feeble, possessing little strength or counsel, so much so that King *Ahaz* himself was driven almost to despair. But *Isaiah*, an extraordinary Prophet <note>Vitringa uses the Latin *Vates*, often implying a divinely inspired poet-prophet.</note>, is sent as a messenger from God to give King *Ahaz* and the whole people, on God's behalf, a most certain hope of victory and preservation. 

Yet the King and the people heard this prophecy with astonishment, because they were conscious of the weakness of the entire Kingdom and they realized that the matter could hardly be achieved without a remarkable miracle. The Prophet *Isaiah* perceived this, and therefore, when he had delivered his prophecy, he said: *Surely you do not believe, because you are not established.* That is: *Although I know that this message of mine is most welcome to you, I can still easily perceive from your faces that you do not have faith in this prophecy of mine, because you are considering the weakness of the kingdom and your own powerlessness. Nevertheless, so that you may have the fullest conviction* <note>original Greek: $\pi\lambda\eta\rho o\phi o\rho\iota\alpha\nu$ (*plērophorian*); a state of complete certainty or full assurance.</note> *of my mission, come now, King Ahaz, ask for a sign from my God on behalf of the whole people, so that not even the slightest scruple or handle for doubting remains for you.* 

I judge this paraphrase <note>original Greek: $\pi\alpha\rho\alpha\phi\rho\alpha\sigma\iota\nu$ (*paraphrasin*)</note> to be easier than all others. We must only prove that this phrasing <note>original Greek: $\phi\rho\alpha\sigma\iota o\lambda o\gamma\iota\alpha$ (*phraseologia*)</note>, *not being established*, signifies the weak and feeble state of the people. And that is indeed not difficult to do. Let us consider that parallel <note>original Greek: $\pi\alpha\rho' \alpha \lambda \lambda \eta \lambda o\nu$ (*par' allēlon*); literally "alongside one another," referring to a cross-reference or parallel passage.</note> passage which the Venerable Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a Dutch theologian known for his "federal theology" and focus on biblical philology.</note> brought forward in his own paraphrase from 2 Chronicles 20:20: **"Believe in the Lord your God, and you shall be established"** <note>original Hebrew: האמינו ביהוה אלהיכם ותאמנו (*Ha’aminu b’Adonai Eloheikhem v’te’amenu*). This is a famous play on words in Hebrew where "faith" and "stability" come from the same root, *A-M-N*.</note>.

<summary>Vitringa provides a historical and psychological context for Isaiah's message to King Ahaz, arguing that the king's lack of faith stemmed from Judah's physical military weakness. ...it seems so evident and manifest to me. This is what must now be pointed out: When we read through the Book of Esther, we notice in it that the Kings of Babylonia <note>Though Esther is set in Persia, Vitringa and his contemporaries often grouped the great Eastern empires together or viewed the Persian kings as successors to the Babylonian throne.</note> had *golden scepters*, or *golden rods*, as the insignias of their power and authority. For the words of the verse that immediately follows our own state: *How has the Oppressor ceased? Has the golden one ceased? Jehovah has broken the rod* <note>original Hebrew: מטה (matteh)</note> *of the Wicked, the scepter* <note>original Hebrew: שבט (shevet)</note> *of the rulers.*

Indeed, this same point can be shown quite clearly from this very verse. For it says: *How has the oppressor* <note>original Hebrew: נגש (nogesh)</note> *ceased? Has the golden one ceased?* Mention is made here of the *Oppressor*: but *scepters*—that is, *rods* and *staffs*—were proper to *Oppressors*, for that is what *shevet* <note>the Hebrew word for scepter or rod</note> signifies. If you doubt it, we have an explicit passage in *Isaiah* chapter 9, verse 4: *For you have broken the rod of his oppressor* <note>original Hebrew: שבט נגש בו (shevet nogesh bo)</note> (of the one demanding from him). It is therefore highly probable that mention would be made in this place of the *Scepter* and the *Rod* where mention is made of the *Oppressor*. To me indeed these things seem so manifest that I do not fear to assert that *madhebah* <note>original Hebrew: מדהבה; often translated as "golden city" or "tribute," but Vitringa argues here for "golden scepter."</note>—*the Golden*—in this place refers to the *Rod* or *golden scepter* of the **King of the Babylonians**, or if you prefer, of him who represented this King of the Babylonians under the New Covenant <note>original Latin: N. Fœdere (Novo Fœdere). Vitringa often interpreted Old Testament prophecies as having a "spiritual" or future fulfillment in the Christian era.</note>, who is compared with the *Oppressor*.

<header>C. VITRINGA</header>

that well-known mark of the Accusative case **את** <note>Hebrew: *et*, a particle marking a definite direct object</note> which is joined to all verbs. Thus **כרת ברית** <note>Hebrew: *karat berit*</note> *struck a covenant*, or more literally, *cut a covenant*; **כרת האשרה** <note>Hebrew: *karat ha-asherah*</note> *He cut down the sacred grove*; **ולא תכרית את חסדך** <note>Hebrew: *ve-lo takhrit et hasdekha*</note> *And you shall not cut off your kindness, that is, your devotion to me*; and there are many more similar examples. If anyone is even slightly skilled in the character and nature of the Hebrew language, they cannot help but think it a very harsh way of speaking for the Hebrews if **כרת** <note>Hebrew: *karat*, meaning "to cut"</note> were constructed with **עלי** <note>Hebrew: *ali*, meaning "upon" or "against"</note>, just as it would be in Latin: *to fall against us* <note>original Latin/Greek: τὸ cadere contra nos</note>, and in Dutch: **To cut off against us.** <note>original Dutch: Tegen ons afhouwen.</note> For it would be much easier to say *who cuts us down* <note>original Hebrew: שכרתנו (she-keratanu)</note> or *falling us*. Since, therefore, the phraseology <note>original Greek: Φρασιολογία (phrasiologia)</note> is both harsh and nowhere used in the Holy Scripture, can anyone find fault with me for seeking a simpler explanation <note>original Greek: ἐξήγησιν (exegesin)</note> of this passage? And indeed, I have found a very easy one, which I believe you would embrace if you understood it. Thus I translate it as follows: *Since you lay down, no one has come up, lopping off our leaves.* In Dutch: **Since you lie down there / no one comes up against us / who would cut off our leaves.** <note>original Dutch: Sint dat ghy daer nederlight / en komt niemant tegen ons op / die onse bladeren afhouwe.</note> Specifically, this is how the matter stands. Anyone who understands this language perceives that the particle **עלי** <note>Hebrew: *ali*</note>, when combined with all kinds of suffixes, is very frequent in the Holy Scripture, and thus the word **עלינו** <note>Hebrew: *alenu*</note> is used six hundred times in that sense <note>Meaning "against us."</note> which all the Interpreters have attached to this passage. Nor should we wonder at this. For this word is so familiar to those who read the scripture that, although they might know another meaning for this word could exist, they never thought of it because of the familiarity of this common meaning. And certainly, it happened no differently to me. For after I made this observation...

# SACRED OBSERVATIONS

I had recorded this idea among my papers two years ago, but I had since forgotten it so completely that I myself must have explained that passage in the traditional way at least twenty times along with all the other interpreters. I would never have recalled this later **paraphrase** <note>original Greek: παράφρασιν, meaning a restatement or alternative interpretation</note> to memory if those same papers had not happened to be at hand. To come to the point, then: no man can doubt that **עָלֵינוּ** <note>Hebrew: *aleinu*</note> can be translated as *our leaves*, since that is a most certain fact. For **עָלֶה** <note>Hebrew: *aleh*</note> means *leaf*, as in Leviticus 26:36: **קוֹל עָלֶה נדף** <note>Hebrew: *kol aleh nidaf*</note> *the sound of a driven leaf*. Also in Isaiah 34:4: **כנבל עָלֶה** <note>Hebrew: *kenabel aleh*</note> *As a leaf falls from the vine*. And in Genesis 3:7: **עֲלֵה תְאֵנָה** <note>Hebrew: *aleh teenah*</note> *Fig leaf*, and many other places. Moreover, **עָלֶה** <note>Hebrew: *aleh*</note> takes the form **עֲלֵי** <note>Hebrew: *alei*</note> in the *plural construct state*, which we recognize from Nehemiah chapter 8:15: **עֲלֵי זַיִת** <note>Hebrew: *alei zayit*</note> *Leaves of the olive tree*. From this, if someone wished to say in Hebrew, *Our leaves*, they could not express it in any other way than as **עָלֵינוּ** <note>Hebrew: *aleinu*</note>, just as we see written here. 

Nor can anyone doubt that this meaning is suitable for this passage; indeed, it is most fitting. The downfall of the King of Babylon is recounted in this **Prophecy** <note>original Latin: *Vaticinio*</note> by means of a certain **Song** <note>original Latin: *Canticum*</note>. And in this **Song**, it is said that all the peoples rejoiced that this King had fallen, because he was not so much a **Commander** <note>original Latin: *Imperator*</note> as he was a cruel and heartless **Oppressor** <note>original Latin: *Exactor*, a harsh collector of tribute or forced labor</note>. Indeed, it is added in this **verse** <note>original Latin: *commate*</note> of ours that even the trees rejoiced—the *fir trees and the cedars of Lebanon*—because he used to not cut them down entirely (as the **Interpreters** commonly maintain; for if they had been cut down completely, they would not be able to rejoice), but he nevertheless used to lop off their foliage and their leaves—that is, their greatest ornament, honor, and glory. For a tree whose leaves fall away...

<meta>This page continues Vitringa's investigation into the title "Desert of the Sea" (Isaiah 21:1). # C. VITRINGA
<meta>catchword: וקרא (And he called)</meta>

<note>original Hebrew: "And he called Babylon 'Desert of the Sea' because Media and Persia were in the northeast of Babylon, as it says, 'I have stirred up [one] from the north' and 'from the rising of the sun' [the east]. Behold, Babylon is west of Media and Persia, and the west is called 'Sea' [Yam]. He says 'desert' because the desert is between Babylon and Media and Persia."</note>

He truly calls Babylon the **Desert of the Sea** <note>original Hebrew: *midbar yam*</note> because the Persians and Medes were in the eastern and northern region (Dutch: **North East**) with respect to **Babylon**. Just as it is said: *I raise him up* (Isaiah 41:25) *from the North, and he shall come from the rising of the Sun.* And behold, **Babylon** is to the west in relation to the **Medes** and **Persians**; however, that which is western is called **Yam** (Sea). He says "desert" because there is a desert between **Babylon**, the **Medes**, and the **Persians**. Thus far **Rabbi David** <note>**David Kimchi** (c. 1160–1235), a famous medieval Jewish grammarian and biblical commentator often cited by Reformation-era scholars</note>, whose reasoning does not seem to be disregarded by me. 

Specifically, what he says is quite certain: namely, that the word **Yam** (Sea) is very often used for "the West" by the Sacred Writers. This is because the Hebrews, who named and divided the entire world according to the boundaries of their own land, had the Mediterranean Sea on their western border. I will add one or two passages. In the book of **Joshua**, chapter 15:12, it is written: *And the western border was the Great Sea* <note>original Hebrew: *ve-gevul yam ha-yam ha-gadol*</note>. Most clearly, however, in the history of **Moses** <note>The Book of Genesis</note>, Book 1, chapter 28:14: *And your offspring shall be like the dust of the earth, and you shall spread out toward the West* <note>original Hebrew: *yamah*</note>, *and the East, and the North, and the South.* 

But it is not only what **Kimchi** asserted that is true; I would also like it noted that **Yam** in the Holy Scriptures is also taken to mean "the South," since they were just as familiar with a sea to the south as they were to the west. It is certainly taken this way by very learned interpreters in **Psalm 107:3**: *And from the lands...* <note>original Hebrew: *u-me-aratzot*</note>

<meta>This page continues Vitringa's analysis of the term "Yam" (Sea) in Hebrew scripture, specifically how it relates to compass directions. # SACRED OBSERVATIONS

<note>original Hebrew: "And from the east and from the west, from the north and from the sea" (Psalm 107:3)</note> *And those whom he gathered from the regions of the East and from the West, from the North and from the sea—**that is, the South.*** The Paraphrast <note>The Aramaic Targum, an ancient translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> correctly states: <note>original Aramaic: "and from the southern sea"</note>. Since it is established as most certain from these documents that *Yam* <note>the Hebrew word for "sea"</note> signifies not only the sea but also the West and the **South**, would it not be permitted for us to translate *Midbar Yam* <note>Isaiah 21:1</note> as the **western desert**, or the **Southern desert**?

In Dutch: **The south or west desert / or, the desert that is toward the west?** Indeed, does not this way of speaking agree much more with sound reason and the genius of the language, and is it therefore not to be preferred over the former interpretation? Everyone certainly understands what a *western desert* is, but what a *desert of the sea* might be remains hidden. 

Furthermore, if the Prophet Isaiah had wished for this *Midbar Yam* to be understood as the waters of the **Euphrates** rendering the region vast and uncultivated, he ought to have said *Yam Ha-Midbar*, **the sea of the desert**, just as we find *Yam Ha-Arabah*, the **Sea of the desert** <note>The Dead Sea</note> in place of *Yam Ha-Melach*, the **Salt Sea**; he would not have said *Midbar Yam*, the **Desert of the sea**. Not to mention that the Euphrates River is constantly called <note>original Greek: *kat’ exochen*</note> *Nahar*, **The River**, preeminently in the sacred texts. There are six hundred such instances. 

However, I cannot imagine that anyone would wish to go against this opinion of mine or criticize the produced version if I can worthily reconcile it with the context itself, upon which the entire hinge of the present matter turns. Let us therefore attempt this now, asking for indulgence if we depart somewhat from our **Kimchi**. Specifically, we do not only accept what our Kimchi noted in his **Interpretation** <note>original Greek: *en Exegesei*</note> concerning the **desert** that existed between **Babylonia**, **Media**, and **Persia**—as that same fact is gathered without difficulty from **Xenophon**, that most excellent writer, who in his *Education of Cyrus*... <note>original Greek: *Kyrou Paideian*</note>

### SACRED OBSERVATIONS

**L I**

into disuse among the Hebrews. Whenever someone released a book or any kind of writing to the public, they were accustomed to recording its subject matter at the head of the pamphlet, much as we do every day. But here is the difference: they usually derived the subject or title of the book from the words or phrases that appeared most prominently in that writing, whereas we derive them from the nature and character of the subject matter itself. This is why the Jews have such strange and unusual <term>titles<gloss>Greek: *epigraphas* (ἐπιγραφὰς)</gloss></term> for their books. 

Let us mention what is well known to everyone. The first book of Moses, which the Greeks called <term>Genesis<gloss>Greek: *geneseōs* (γενέσεως)</gloss></term> <note>Meaning 'Origin' or 'Birth'.</note>, was called by them <term>Bereshit<gloss>Hebrew: בראשית</gloss></term>—*In the beginning.* What a strange title, you might say! And yet it arose from no other source than the fact that this little book begins with the word *Bereshit*. 

However, although the entire book was named by later Jews after its first word, we should not assume they always named a book after the very first word of a manuscript; if they perceived a greater <term>emphasis<gloss>Greek: *emphasis* (ἔμφασις)</gloss></term> in subsequent words, they preferred those. This is not difficult to prove. Indeed, the second volume written by Moses is called <term>Shemot<gloss>Hebrew: שמות</gloss></term> <note>Meaning 'Names'.</note> by the Jews, because they felt there was a greater emphasis in this word than in the first word, which was <term>Ve-eleh<gloss>Hebrew: ואלה</gloss></term> <note>Meaning 'And these'.</note>. 

This is even clearer in the fourth volume, called <term>Bemidbar<gloss>Hebrew: במדבר</gloss></term> <note>Meaning 'In the wilderness'; this refers to the Book of Numbers.</note>, even though the word *Bemidbar* follows after several other words. We believe this is exactly what happened here and in other prophecies. For the word <term>Vision<gloss>Hebrew: *chizayon* (חזיון)</gloss></term> appears in the first verse of this chapter. And because no more suitable word had come before it, the entire prophecy was named after it. Hence, I would translate <term>Massa Ge Chizayon<gloss>Hebrew: משא גי חזיון</gloss></term> as: *Pro-*

# C. VITRINGA

...pronouncement regarding the valley of vision. <note>original: "latio de valle visionis"</note> This is the kind of prophecy in which mention is made of the "valley of vision." For although I do not deny that this pronouncement or sentence was directed against this valley of vision, I do not think it can be concluded from these words alone, based on what has been said previously. For it often happens that many conclusions drawn by others from certain words are true, even if they are poorly concluded from the specific force of those words. In Dutch we would express this best as: **An utterance (of God) concerning the valley of vision / or, dealing with the valley of vision.** <note>original Dutch: "Een uytspraeck (Godts) aengaende het dal der gesichte / vel, handelende van 't dal der gesichte."</note>

Indeed, if we consider the matter correctly, we might perhaps establish, not without reason, that many titles of the Prophecies were not added by those very Prophets who conceived them by Divine will, but perhaps by other holy men. These were the individuals put in charge of reviewing those sacred scriptures for the Jewish people—texts which were formerly stored in the Temple or copied for private use. And surely there is no fault or error to be found in that possibility. For if we assume that all the titles and <term>inscriptions<gloss>Greek: *epigraphas* (ἐπιγραφὰς)</gloss></term> of the Books of both the Old and New Testaments <note>The "Instrumenti" refers to the "Instruments" or Testaments of the Bible.</note> were added by other holy men, why should we not think the same of certain individual prophecies, which we now read adorned with titles and inscriptions? 

If this was indeed the case, can we imagine it was done by them in any way other than what they were accustomed to? As has just been proven, they were accustomed—frequently (though I do not deny other examples occur)—when assigning inscriptions, not so much to look at the overall content of the writing as to the specific words, <term>phrases<gloss>Greek: *phraseis* (φράσεις)</gloss></term>, and other more notable things that were first mentioned in that text.

### SACRED OBSERVATIONS.

...has been correctly introduced. Regarding the word **ʿênayim** <note>Hebrew: עינים</note>, I think it can certainly be translated as **fountains**. Indeed, this word occurs with that meaning in Moses’ first book, chapter 38, verse 14: *And she sat at the opening of the **fountains**, which are on the way toward Timnah.* <note>Genesis 38:14. In modern translations, this is often left as a place name, "Enaim," but Vitringa follows the literal meaning of the roots.</note> I translate **ʿênayim** in this passage as *fountains*, since interpreters generally understand two fountains by this term.

For the word is in the **dual** number <term>dual: a grammatical form used in languages like Hebrew to denote exactly two of something, distinct from the singular or the plural</term>. But I am not the only one to do this, as Onkelos <note>Onkelos was a famous 1st-century convert to Judaism credited with the Targum Onkelos, the primary Aramaic translation of the Torah.</note> agrees with me, who translates the phrase here as: *In the division of the fountains.* <note>original Aramaic: בפרשות עינין (*Be-parashat aynin*)</note> Nor does it seem to me that he did this without reason, since not only is the dual sometimes used in place of the plural, but a reason for that specific usage can be given here.

Specifically, **ʿayin** <note>Hebrew: עין</note> in the singular number signifies a **fountain** among the Hebrews, just as it also signifies an **eye**: for the opening of a fountain has the shape of an eye. This is most certain and cannot be doubted by any person. Furthermore, since **ʿayin** is inflected in the dual as **ʿênayim**—because humans are endowed with a pair of eyes—it should be known that such is the character of the Hebrew language that words which are dual by their nature can be used to express not only a pair, but also a plural number. If this is correctly observed, I believe all difficulty is resolved.

I will make this matter manifest with clearly similar examples. There is such a passage in Moses’ third book, chapter 11, verse 13: *And every winged reptile which has **four feet**.* <note>Leviticus 11:21 (Vitringa cites verse 13, but the description of four-footed winged creatures appears later in the chapter). The Hebrew uses the word *raglayim*.</note> **Raglayim** <note>Hebrew: רגלים</note> is in the dual number. Do you think, then, it should be translated as "which has four *pairs* of feet"? Certainly no one has reached such a level of madness yet. Therefore, **raglayim** is taken as if it were written as a plural, because nature...

Who, then, can find fault with me for translating *ʿênayim* in this place as **fountains**, rather than as "two fountains"? For since *ʿênayim* signifies fountains because the openings of springs are similar to eyes, and because nature has given us a twin eye, it follows that the word *ʿênayim*—even if it enjoys the meaning of "fountains"—both can and should be explained as a plural, despite having a dual termination. 

I think these points are now sufficiently manifest. Since it is certain that those first words can support that interpretation, we must further understand that the parable simultaneously becomes most fitting. For no one ought to be surprised that there are fountains in a stone. A most clear allusion is made here to the waters that came forth from the **rock** and the **cliff** in the desert, of which there is such frequent mention in sacred matters. Lexicographers provide countless examples, which I refrain from listing here, since they are most well-known and familiar.

But this same word *Gamar* also has the meaning of **TEACHING** and learning, and for that reason, it was frequent among the people of that time. For the Paraphrasts used that speech which was common at the time, since they translated the Holy Book from the Hebrew language into the vernacular. Let us prove this indeed. Thus in **Job XXII. 22.** in the *Chaldæan Paraphrase*: **LEARN** <note>original: גמר כדן (*gamar kedan*)</note> now the Law from his mouth. And in **Deut VI. 7.** in the same Chaldæan version: And you shall **TEACH** <note>original: ותגמרון (*ve-tagmeron*)</note> those words to your sons. In this sense, it also occurs frequently in the Talmudic Code.

With these things established, we say that the word *pleroo* <note>original: πληρόω</note>, corresponding precisely to the mentioned word *Gamar*, takes on those meanings for which *Gamar* is typically used. For this is a constant habit of the writers of the New Covenant: to take Greek words, if they agree in their primary meaning with Hebrew words, and bend them toward the other meanings of those Hebrew words derived from the primary one. For many opinions and expositions of the Holy Scripture can contain most certain truths, even if they are poorly applied to this or that specific passage.

Perhaps, however, that passage in Saint Paul’s Second Epistle to Timothy, chapter 3:17, can also be reduced to this way of speaking: "that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work" <note>original Greek: ἵνα ἄρτιος ᾖ ὁ τοῦ Θεוῦ ἄνθρωπος, πρὸς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν ἐξηρτισμένος</note>. This means that the man of God should be **PERFECT**, or **PERFECTLY INSTRUCTED**, for every good work. For the Greek words for "complete" and "equipped" <note>original: ἄρτιος and ἐξηρτισμένος</note> correspond to the Hebrew word *gamar* <note>original: גמר; meaning to complete, perfect, or teach</note>, so that to be *perfect, fulfilled,* or *consummated* is nothing other than to be **WELL EDUCATED**. For the Apostle had spoken there about the "sacred writings" <note>original Greek: περὶ τῶν γραμμάτων</note>, since they were able to make one "wise unto salvation" <note>original Greek: σοφίσαι εἰς σωτηρίαν</note>.

Nor is it only the word *gamar* that we can apply to this context, but also the word *shalam* <note>original Hebrew/Aramaic: שלם; typically meaning peace or wholeness</note>, which enjoys a meaning not much different. Indeed, the Syrian Translator <note>The Peshitta, an ancient Syriac translation of the Bible</note> joined those two words here in an excellent way. It is a version worthy of being written out. It reads: "That the man of God may be perfect, for every good work completed" <note>original Syriac: דנהוא גמיר ברנשא דאלהא לכל עבד טבו משלמן</note>. This corresponds entirely to the Greek. 

Certainly, the word *shalam* in the *Aphel* form <note>A specific grammatical structure in Semitic languages (like Hebrew and Syriac) that indicates causing an action to happen; here, it refers to causing a teaching to be "completed" by handing it over</note> signifies "to hand over," and specifically "to hand over doctrines," which is the opposite of "receiving" <note>original Greek: τῷ παραλαμβάνειν</note>. I learned this very thing from Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 11:23. The Greek reads: "For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you" <note>original Greek: Ἐγὼ γὰר παρέλαβον ἀπὸ τοῦ Κυρίου ὃ καὶ παρέדωκα ὑμῖν</note>. The Syrian translated it in this manner: "For I received from our Lord that which I delivered to you" <note>original Syriac: אנא גיר קבלת מן מרן הו מדם דאשלמת לכון</note>. Since these points are obvious, I will not pursue them further.

"...and you decorate the monuments of the righteous" <note>original Greek: καὶ κοσμεῖτε τὰ μνημεῖα τῶν δικαίων; a reference to Matthew 23:29</note>. I had thought to add some illustrations of these **decorated tombs** from the Tractate *Shekalim* <note>A section of the Mishnah concerning the collection of the Temple tax and related communal expenses</note>, a work I had labored on translating once before I realized it had already been rearranged by others. However, I will pass over those things now, as I have noticed they were already brought forward by the most diligent *Lightfoot* <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675), a renowned English Hebraist and scholar of the Talmud</note>. Nevertheless, I will present one passage from that same tractate which, though observed by those same learned men, has not, in my judgment, been quite correctly understood. It is found in the *Shekalim* Code, Chapter II, Section 5: *The surplus [money] for a dead person goes to his heirs; this is the view of Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Nathan says: The surplus of the dead shall be left until Elijah comes. Rabbi Nathan [also] says: From the surplus of the dead, they build a monument over his grave.*

**The surplus for the dead goes to his heirs.** (This means that if there were any leftover drachmas <note>ancient coins</note> from a sum paid for a person's needs which they did not receive before they died, that remainder is to be transferred to the heirs as part of the deceased's estate.) **Rabbi Meir says: The surplus of the dead should be left until Elijah comes.** <note>A common Jewish legal phrase meaning the matter is undecided and must wait for the prophet Elijah to resolve it in the messianic age</note>. **Rabbi Nathan says: From the surplus of the dead, they build a <term>nephesh</term> [monument] over his grave.**

It is truly a marvel that the word *nephesh* <note>original Hebrew: נפש</note> signifies a **sepulchral monument** in this context, since among the Hebrews, Chaldeans <note>Aramaic-speakers</note>, and Syrians, it consistently denotes the **Soul** and whatever is or was **animated**. And yet, this meaning is certain not only from this passage but from others as well. There is a very famous saying found in both the Gemara <note>The component of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis</note> and in *Bereshit Rabba* <note>A midrashic collection of interpretations on the Book of Genesis</note>: *One does not make sepulchral monuments for the righteous, for their words are their memorial.* 

Although I do not doubt that this specific meaning of the word originally flowed from the first passage cited, it is certainly due to the rarity of this word being used in this sense that it has led to various...

We read that Absalom, while still alive, created a memorial for himself. <note>Referring to 2 Samuel 18:18, where Absalom sets up a pillar in the King’s Valley because he had no son to keep his name in remembrance.</note> We will not attempt to prove this further, as it is a most certain fact. This seems likely to us, but at present, we do not have the documents at hand to firmly establish it. 

Yet, if you are unwilling to accept this, I would say that this formula is ordinarily inscribed on those monuments: <note>original Hebrew: נשמתה תהא צרורה בגן עדן אא'ס סלה (*Nishmatah tehe tzerurah be-gan eden...*)</note> *May his soul be bound in the Garden of Eden, Amen, Amen, Amen, Selah.* (I suspect the ancients may have used the word *soul* <note>original Hebrew: נפש (*Nefesh*)</note> just as those same Jews otherwise speak). However, I believe I can gather from a certain illustrious passage in the book of **Jesus Sirach** <note>Also known as the Book of Ecclesiasticus, a work of ethical teachings from the 2nd century BCE</note> that this formula for epitaphs is not recent, but very ancient. I will review and illustrate the passage. He discusses it thus in chapter 36, verse 26: <note>original Greek: Ὁ κτώμενος γυναῖκα ἐνάρχεται κτήσεως, βοηθὸν καθ' αὑτὸν καὶ στύλον ἀναπαύσεως.</note> *He who has acquired a wife begins a possession, a helper suitable for himself and a pillar of rest.* 

**Drusius** <note>Joannes Drusius (1550–1616), a Flemish Protestant scholar and expert in Oriental languages</note> translates it this way: *He who has acquired a wife has the beginning of a possession, an aid fit for himself, and a column of quiet*; and he notes that "pillar of rest" is said in Hebrew as <note>original Hebrew: עמוד מנוח (*Amud menuach*)</note>; because only then does a man rest, once he has taken a wife. I would not wish to oppose this too vehemently, yet I believe this phrase carries a greater **emphasis**. The **Dutch Interpreters** <note>Referring to the translators of the *Statenvertaling*, the standard Dutch Bible</note> have: *A place where one may rest.* <note>original Dutch: Een plaet / daer men op rusten mach.</note> But surely "pillar" <note>original Greek: στύλος (*stylos*)</note> and "column" <note>original Hebrew: עמוד (*amud*)</note> signify something else entirely.

I am quite of the opinion that in this passage, an allusion is made to those **grave markers** <term>cippos: small stone pillars or posts used as monuments</term> and **columns** that were erected for the dead, upon which was inscribed the word *Rest* <note>original Hebrew: מנוח (Menu'ach)</note>, as we noted in the previous epitaph. This was done either to indicate that *the Soul of this or that man might rest there*, or because that specific formula, *May his rest be in the Garden of Eden*, was recorded upon them. These columns were called *pillars of rest* <note>original Greek: στύλοι ἀναπαύσεως (styloi anapauseos)</note> or *of rests*, as is read in certain Manuscripts; a reading which, according to our explanation, is not at all inappropriate.

If this interpretation of ours is admitted, the <unclear>paraphrase</unclear> <note>The Greek term is likely παράφρασις (paraphrasis)</note> of this saying will be very easy. Namely, it suggests that a man who has obtained a wife possesses a most certain place and sign of his rest, just as the pillars of the deceased are signs of those who rest, and the dead rest beside their pillars. For a man who has not yet taken a wife is similar to those people who wander everywhere, lacking a fixed seat for their soul—that is, for their desire. Once they have attained this "seat" through marriage, they are able to settle themselves into rest, just like the bodies resting at their grave markers. This expression appears to me to be *most emphatic* <note>original Greek: ἐμφατικωτάτη (emphatikotatē)</note>.

Just as these grave markers were called *pillars of rest*, I would also think that these columns, or whatever funeral monuments they were, were called *Souls* <note>original Hebrew: נפשות (Nefashot)</note> because the first word found inscribed upon them was *Soul* <note>original Hebrew: נפש (Nefesh)</note>. Thus, the word "Soul" signifies a **grave marker** upon which was inscribed: *May the SOUL of this person rest*, or, *May it be bound in the bundle with all the righteous* <note>A reference to 1 Samuel 25:29, a common Jewish blessing for the deceased</note>. It was observed, therefore, by the most learned **Caninius** <note>Angelo Canini (1521–1557), a noted Italian grammarian and linguist</note> in the fourth chapter of his *Annotations on certain passages of the New Testament*, that the bundle of willow and other trees which was bound together during the **Feast of Tabernacles** <term>σκηνοπηγίας (skēnopēgias): the Jewish festival of Sukkot, where participants dwell in booths and carry branches</term> was called a **Hosanna**. But, you will ask, why was a bundle of willows called a "Hosanna," which means "Save, I pray"? I shall explain this most clearly. The Jews were accustomed to celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles with the greatest joy, and to bind together bundles of various trees, with which they ran about exulting. While running about, they would sing a certain song which began with **Hosanna**, that is, *Save, I pray, O Lord*. And from this, the bundle made of tree branches was itself called a "save, I pray." # SACRED OBSERVATIONS
<note>original Latin: *OBSERVATIONES SACRÆ*</note>

...our father, to give to us. That we, being delivered from the hand of our enemies, might serve him without fear. <note>original Greek: τὸν πατέρα ἡμῶν τοῦ δοῦναι ἡμῖν. Ἀφόβως ἐκ χειρὸς τῶν ἐχθρῶν ὑμῶν ῥυσθέντας λατρεύειν αὐτῷ. This is from the Song of Zechariah in Luke 1:73-74.</note> When I once turned my mind to this passage, it seemed to me to be **poorly punctuated**, as it is currently read; it is a wonder that **Beza** <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605) was a major Protestant reformer and scholar known for his influential editions of the Greek New Testament</note> and other distinguished men whom I have consulted did not notice it. I therefore read and punctuate it thus: *The oath which he swore to Abraham our father, to grant to us that we, being delivered from the hand of our enemies, might serve him without fear.* <note>original Greek: Ὅρκου, ὃν ὤμοσε πρὸς Ἀβραὰμ τὸν πατέρα ἡμῶν, τοῦ δοῦναι ἡμῖν ἀφόβως ἐκ χειρὸς τῶν ἐχθρῶν ἡμῶν ῥυσθέντας λατρεύειν αὐτῷ.</note>

In this way, the phrase "to give" <note>original Greek: τὸ δοῦναι</note> does not refer back to the "oath" <note>original Greek: ὅρκου</note>, but rather to the "serving without fear" <note>original Greek: τὸ λατρεύειν ἀφόβως</note>. Certainly, I do not think it is either a Hebrew or a Greek idiom to say *to give someone an oath* in place of *to fulfill an oath*. Nor, certainly, does the passage cited here by the venerable **Beza** from the fifth book of **Moses** <note>referring to the book of Deuteronomy</note>, chapter 26:3, prove anything. For this most learned man seems to have intended something else when he brought it forward. It reads thus: *When I come into the land which the Lord swore to our fathers to give to us.* <note>original Hebrew: כי באתי אל הארץ אשר נשבע יהוה לאבותינו לתת לנו</note> It is manifest to anyone from the first inspection of that passage that the word **"to give"** refers to **"the land promised by the oath,"** but not to the oath itself. 

But indeed, that phrasing which is found in my proposed punctuation—**"to give us to serve"** <note>original Latin: τὸ δοῦναι ἡμῖν λατρεύειν</note>—is so frequent among the Hebrews and the Greeks in the manuscripts of both Covenants <note>the Old and New Testaments</note> that it occurs everywhere. For them, the word **"give"** <note>original Hebrew: נתן (natan) or Greek: δίδωμι (didōmi)</note> is used in those places for **"to cause"** or **"to promise"** so that something *is* or *might be done* in this or that way; and it is constructed with a following verb in the infinitive mood. I will add some evidence so that the reliability of this matter may be absolutely certain. 

Psalm 16:10: *You will not give your pious one to see corruption.* <note>original Hebrew: לא תתן חסידך לראות שחת</note> Word for word: *You will not give your pious one to see corruption*, but the sense is: *You will not cause that*...

<meta>This page continues Vitringa's analysis of how the Greek text of the New Testament reflects the underlying Hebrew and Aramaic thought patterns of its authors. Having discussed the verb "to give," he now moves to a linguistic analysis of the word "blood" and its double meaning in the Semitic languages of the time.</meta>

SACRED OBSERVATIONS. 289

...it is certain that, since these things are written in Greek, they have regard for that **dialect** which the Jews used at that time, as we have already remarked several times. Indeed, if we consider this, we notice a most delightful *emphasis* <note>original Greek: ἔμφασιν (*emphasin*)</note> in the word *blood* <note>original Greek: αἷμα (*haima*)</note>, which corresponds to the Syriac *damyn* <note>דמין</note> and is the plural of *dam* <note>דם</note> / and which signifies *Blood*. For it must be assumed that the Hebrews and Syrians said not only *dam*, but also *damim* and *damyn*. Thus in Genesis 4:18 <note>The citation in the source is 4:18, though the quote is from Genesis 4:10</note>: *The voice of your brother’s bloods crying out* <note>original Hebrew: קול דמי אחיך צעקים (*Kol demei achicha tzoakim*)</note>, which nevertheless the most excellent Author of the Epistle to the Hebrews translates through *blood* <note>αἷμα</note> in chapter 12:14 <note>Likely referring to Hebrews 12:24, regarding the blood of Abel</note>. But that *the blood* <note>τὸ αἷμα</note> in this place looks back to *damyn* in the plural number seems likely to me, because Saint Paul here refers to the *shedding of the blood of Christ* performed on the cross. Now, that *shedding of blood* (called *haimatekchysia* <note>αἱματεκχυσία</note> by the writer to the Hebrews) was expressed by the Hebrews as *shefichut damim* <note>שפיכות דמים</note>, the *shedding of bloods*, not *shefichut dam* <note>שפיכות דם</note>, the *shedding of blood* [singular]. Indeed, where the shedding of blood was great, such as it was in Christ, they expressed it through *damyn*. Relevant here is a passage which is in *Niddah*, chapter 9 <note>The Niddah is a tractate of the Talmud concerning ritual purity</note>: *Whichever woman’s bloods (menstrual) are many, her children are many.* This also occurs in the Holy Book. If we grant these things, it must be understood that the same word *damyn* signifies *price* among the Chaldeans and Syrians, which was certainly most familiar in the age of our Lord. There are many examples among the Paraphrasts <note>Translators of the Aramaic Targums, which were common Jewish Bible translations</note>. Take this one, which is in *Isaiah chapter 55*: *And learn without price.* <note>original Aramaic: ואליפו בלא בדמין (*v’alifu bela bidmin*)</note>. There is, therefore, a most sweet wordplay in the word *blood* <note>αἷμα</note>, in that it signifies a kind of blood which is simultaneously a *price*. How beautifully Peter joined these things...

Yet have those men themselves followed the true explanation of these words? In Dutch, we express this perfectly as: **The upper city.** <note>original Dutch: De boven stadt.</note> If you are even moderately practiced in reading this most excellent writer, you cannot be ignorant of this.

# C. VITRINGA

*Flacius* <note>Matthias Flacius Illyricus (1520–1575) was a prominent Lutheran reformer and theologian known for his work on biblical hermeneutics, the *Clavis Scripturae* (Key to the Scripture).</note> discusses this in the *Key to the Scripture, part 1*. All in this place translate that Greek preposition **hyper** <note>original Greek: ὑπὲρ</note> with the preposition **THROUGH** <note>Latin: *per*</note>; whereas it should rather be understood and translated in its native meaning as **CONCERNING** <note>Latin: *de*</note>, just as *Luther* alone translated it in the common tongue <note>Referring to Martin Luther's German translation of the Bible.</note>. For there the *Apostle* indicates the matter or argument—the subject he wishes to pray for or advise the *Thessalonians* about—namely, *concerning the final judgment*, so they do not think it is already at hand and thus become recklessly agitated. *Wherefore other translators either make the text mutilated and obscure, or are even forced to add words of their own.* I would not wish to be as severe a critic as this most learned man is—whose temperament we have come to know from his actions—though I judge that his transposition <note>the re-ordering of the sentence structure for clarity</note> alone is to be approved, as it is the only true one. Thus, I conceive the Greek words in this way:

### SACRED OBSERVATIONS.

For we cannot persuade ourselves otherwise than that to compare these interpretations with one another is to praise the latter. For what kind of <term>phraseology (Φρασιολογία)</term> is this: *To ask by the coming of Christ?* <note>original Latin: "Rogare per adventum Christi?"</note> Which of the sacred writers has ever spoken in such a way? Certainly, in the interpretation of words, one should not look to see if phrases can be reduced to some awkward sense through many twists and turns, but rather we must accept that which is easiest of all, and natural both to the spirit of the language and the common thoughts of that age.

Next, can the particle **hyper** <note>original Greek: ὑπὲρ</note> be translated as **THROUGH** or **BY**? <note>original Latin: "per"</note> I truly do not think it is used in such a way in the entire New Testament; nor have instances yet occurred in the works of approved Greek authors in which I have observed this use of the little word. Meaningful definitions of words are not to be forged at our own whim, but are to be perceived and learned from the sacred books themselves. 

But our transposition <note>the re-ordering of the sentence for clarity mentioned on the previous page</note> will be much more evident if we consider the passage itself and its occasion a little more closely. Paul the Apostle had sent an Epistle to the Thessalonians before this other one (which is now called the "First"), and in it he had discussed at length the glorious coming of Christ the Lord for judgment. However, he had spoken of that coming in such a way that less-educated men might think they could conclude from his words that this coming of Christ the Lord would happen very soon. 

This will appear very evident to us if we weigh chapter 4, verse 15 of the preceding Epistle. Paul argues in that place: *For this we say to you by the word of the Lord, that we who are alive and remain until the coming of the Lord will not precede those who have fallen asleep.* <note>original Greek: τοῦτο γὰρ ὑμῖν λέγομεν ἐν λόγῳ Κυρίου ὅτι ἡμεῖς οἱ ζῶντες οἱ περιλειπόμενοι εἰς τὴν παρουσίαν Κυρίου οὐ μὴ φθάσωμεν τοὺς κοιμηθέντας.</note> And at verse 17: *Then we who are alive and remain will be caught up together with them in the clouds into the...* <note>original Greek: Ἔπειτα ἡμεῖς οἱ ζῶνtes οἱ περιλειπόμενοι ἅμα σὺν αὐτοῖς ἁρπαγησόμεθα ἐν νεφέλαις εἰς ἀ-</note>

<header>C. VITRINGA</header>

The Greek word for "so" <note>original Greek: οὕτως</note> was certainly not accurately <note>original Greek: ἀκριβῶς</note> introduced into the text by the venerable *Beza*, despite his great talent and learning. This choice resulted in later interpreters following him and treating the words of verses four and five not as a description of the subject—namely, "the one who teaches a different doctrine" <note>original Greek: τοῦ ἑτεροδιδασκαλοῦντος</note>—but as a predicate <note>The "predicate" is the part of the sentence that makes a statement about the subject. Vitringa argues that these verses are meant to describe the person's character, not just state a fact about them.</note>.

For I am not only disputing the fact that the little word "not" <note>original Greek: οὐ</note> is understood as being implied there, but also that the content of those verses is being treated as the main statement. I certainly judge that this version is not only contrary to the grammatical construction, but it also strips all the power and emphasis <note>original Greek: ἔμφασιν</note> from the Apostle’s own words. For what mortal can claim a sentence is deficient if the sentence already possesses its own inherent power? Who would tolerate the insertion of words or particles into the text if there were no urgent necessity for it?

But in truth, far from any necessity demanding such an addition, the entire context actually flows much more easily—and possesses a far greater emphasis—if that insertion is removed. Indeed, if we take the phrase "he is puffed up" <note>original Greek: τὸ τετύφωται</note> as the main statement, do we really see a fitting <note>original Greek: πρέπον</note> connection in the Apostle’s words? Is it true that everyone who "teaches a different doctrine" <note>original Greek: ἑτεροδιδασκαλεῖ</note> is always "puffed up with pride" <note>original Greek: τετύφωται</note>? Might someone not teach a different doctrine simply out of ignorance, perhaps because they were not fully convinced of the previous teaching?

Furthermore, is "the one teaching a different doctrine" <note>original Greek: ὁ ἑτεροδιδασκαλῶν</note> always occupied with useless questions, or obsessed by them? Does it not often happen that a God-fearing person might sometimes have doubts about questions of great importance and interpret them differently? Such a person, acting as is proper, certainly cannot be rightly called "swollen with pride" and "knowing nothing" <note>original Greek: μηδὲν ἐπίστασθαι</note>. We see, therefore, that this common interpretation weakens the Apostle’s Speech. There are also those final words, "withdraw yourself from such people" <note>original Greek: ἀφίστασο ἀπὸ τῶν τοιούτων</note>, which are entangled in the same sequence of the discourse...
